name: Green Giant Arborvitae
water: Moderate — weekly until established, then drought tolerant
description: Green Giant Arborvitae (Thuja standishii x plicata) is the fastest-growing evergreen screen commonly planted in Gwinnett County, adding 3 to 5 feet per year until it reaches a mature height of 30 to 40 feet with a dense pyramidal habit 12 to 18 feet wide. Unlike Leyland Cypress, it resists bagworms and Seiridium canker, the two problems that shorten the life of screening conifers in Atlanta-metro heat and humidity. Its rich green, scale-like foliage holds color through winter without bronzing. Georgia's heavy clay soil is not a problem as long as the planting hole is graded for drainage, since Green Giant tolerates clay far better than most arborvitae cultivars but still resents standing water. Once established, roughly two growing seasons, it needs no supplemental water except during extended summer drought. Because a single row spaced 5 to 6 feet apart forms a solid privacy wall within 3 to 4 years, it is the plant we recommend most often for new-construction lot lines and HOA screening requirements in Lawrenceville subdivisions.
plantingTips: Plant in spring or fall in a hole twice the width of the root ball but no deeper, since Georgia's red clay drains slowly and a too-deep hole becomes a bathtub that drowns roots. Backfill with the native soil (amending heavily is discouraged, it can create a perched water table), mulch 2-3 inches deep keeping mulch off the trunk, and water deeply twice a week for the first two months. Space plants 5-6 feet apart center to center for a solid screen within a few years.
fastFacts: Mature height: 30-40 ft, width 12-18 ft
Growth rate: 3-5 ft per year, among the fastest privacy conifers
Resistant to bagworms and canker that plague Leyland Cypress
Full sun to part shade, tolerates Georgia clay if drained
Deer resistant and evergreen year-round
Recommended spacing: 5-6 ft apart for a solid privacy wall

faqs.question: How fast does Green Giant Arborvitae grow?
faqs.answer: Green Giant Arborvitae grows 3 to 5 feet per year under good conditions, making it the fastest common privacy evergreen for Georgia yards. A newly planted 7-gallon specimen can reach 12-15 feet within 4-5 years, forming a mature screen faster than Leyland Cypress or Emerald Green Arborvitae.

faqs.question: How far apart should I plant Green Giant Arborvitae for privacy?
faqs.answer: Space Green Giant Arborvitae 5 to 6 feet apart on center for a continuous privacy screen. Planting closer than 5 feet crowds root systems and increases disease risk in Georgia's humid summers, while spacing wider than 6 feet leaves visible gaps for the first several years.

faqs.question: Is Green Giant Arborvitae deer resistant?
faqs.answer: Yes, Green Giant Arborvitae is considered deer resistant, though hungry deer in a hard winter may browse young, unestablished plants. Its dense scale-like foliage is less palatable than Arborvitae 'Emerald Green,' and established plantings in Gwinnett County landscapes rarely show significant deer damage.

name: Nellie R. Stevens Holly
water: Moderate — weekly until established, then drought tolerant
bloomSeason: N/A (small spring flowers, grown for foliage and berries)
description: Nellie R. Stevens Holly (Ilex x 'Nellie R. Stevens') is a hybrid between English Holly and Chinese Holly that produces glossy, dark-green, lightly spined foliage and a dense pyramidal form reaching 15 to 25 feet tall and 10 to 15 feet wide. It is self-fruiting, meaning a single plant sets its heavy crop of bright red winter berries without a separate male pollinator, which is not true of most hollies. This makes it one of the most reliable screening and specimen plants for Lawrenceville landscapes where homeowners want privacy plus winter berry color for birds. It handles Georgia's clay soil and summer humidity better than boxwood or laurel, and shows strong resistance to the leaf spot and root rot issues common in wet Piedmont clay. Growth is moderate to fast at 2 to 3 feet per year, slower than Green Giant Arborvitae but denser and more formal in habit, which is why it is frequently chosen for foundation screens and property-line hedges that need to stay narrower than a fast conifer.
plantingTips: Site in full sun to part shade in well-drained soil; in heavy Gwinnett County clay, plant slightly high (the top of the root ball 1-2 inches above grade) and mound soil to the sides rather than digging deep. Water deeply twice weekly the first growing season. For a hedge, space plants 6-8 feet apart; for a single specimen, allow 10-15 feet of clearance. Light shaping after the spring flush encourages denser branching.
fastFacts: Mature height: 15-25 ft, width 10-15 ft
Self-fruiting — no male holly needed for red winter berries
Growth rate: 2-3 ft per year
Evergreen, glossy dark green foliage with light spines
Deer resistant, tolerates Georgia clay and summer heat
Berries are toxic if ingested by pets — not pet safe

faqs.question: Does Nellie R. Stevens Holly need a male plant to produce berries?
faqs.answer: No, Nellie R. Stevens Holly is self-fruiting and produces its bright red berries without a separate male pollinator plant. This sets it apart from most holly species and is a major reason it's favored for reliable winter color in Georgia landscapes.

faqs.question: How tall does Nellie R. Stevens Holly get?
faqs.answer: Nellie R. Stevens Holly typically matures to 15-25 feet tall and 10-15 feet wide, though it can be pruned and maintained shorter as a formal hedge. Left unpruned it forms a dense pyramidal tree, making it suitable for tall privacy screens or as a specimen.

faqs.question: Is Nellie R. Stevens Holly toxic to dogs?
faqs.answer: Yes, the berries and leaves of Nellie R. Stevens Holly can cause vomiting, diarrhea, and stomach upset if pets ingest them. Plant it away from areas where dogs graze on fallen berries, and rake up dropped berries near pet play areas.

name: Emerald Green Arborvitae
water: Moderate — regular water needed, less drought tolerant than Green Giant
description: Emerald Green Arborvitae (Thuja occidentalis 'Smaragd') is a narrow, columnar conifer that grows 12 to 15 feet tall but only 3 to 4 feet wide, making it the go-to choice when a customer needs a tight evergreen screen in a narrow side yard where Green Giant Arborvitae would grow too wide. Its foliage stays bright emerald-green year-round rather than bronzing in winter like many arborvitae. Growth is slow to moderate at 6 to 9 inches per year, so it takes longer to fill in than Green Giant but requires far less lateral space and rarely needs shearing to maintain its natural columnar shape. In Georgia's clay soil it performs best with a well-drained planting site, since Emerald Green is more prone to root rot in soggy conditions than the more vigorous Green Giant. Deer will browse it more readily than Green Giant Arborvitae, so it is best used in fenced yards or areas without heavy deer pressure in the Lawrenceville area.
plantingTips: Choose a site with excellent drainage; if your Gwinnett County lot has heavy clay, amend a wide planting area or build a slightly raised bed rather than digging a single deep hole. Space plants 3-4 feet apart for a tight, uniform screen. Water two to three times weekly during the first summer, since Emerald Green is less drought tolerant than other arborvitae once established. Avoid deer-prone, unfenced areas.
fastFacts: Mature height: 12-15 ft, width only 3-4 ft — ideal for narrow spaces
Slower growth than Green Giant: 6-9 inches per year
Naturally columnar, needs little to no shearing
Not deer resistant — best in fenced yards
Prefers consistently moist, well-drained soil
Evergreen bright green color year-round, no winter bronzing

faqs.question: What is the difference between Emerald Green and Green Giant Arborvitae?
faqs.answer: Emerald Green Arborvitae stays narrow at 3-4 feet wide and grows slowly (6-9 in/year), ideal for tight side yards, while Green Giant grows fast (3-5 ft/year) to 12-18 feet wide and needs more space. Emerald Green is also less drought tolerant and more deer-susceptible than Green Giant.

faqs.question: How far apart should Emerald Green Arborvitae be planted?
faqs.answer: Plant Emerald Green Arborvitae 3 to 4 feet apart on center for a dense, continuous privacy screen. Because it stays narrow at maturity, this tighter spacing works well without the crowding issues that wider-growing evergreens face at the same distance.

faqs.question: Do deer eat Emerald Green Arborvitae?
faqs.answer: Yes, deer readily browse Emerald Green Arborvitae, especially newly planted specimens in fall and winter when other food is scarce. In Gwinnett County areas with heavy deer traffic, protect young plants with fencing or repellent, or choose the more deer-resistant Green Giant instead.

name: Leyland Cypress
water: Moderate until established, then drought tolerant
description: Leyland Cypress (x Hesperotropsis leylandii) has been the classic fast privacy tree across the Atlanta metro for decades, capable of 3 to 4 feet of growth per year and reaching 40 to 60 feet at maturity with soft, blue-green, feathery foliage. It remains an excellent choice for large properties that need a tall, fast screen and have the 15-20 feet of width to accommodate it. The tradeoff homeowners should know before planting: Leyland Cypress is more susceptible than Green Giant Arborvitae to Seiridium and Botryosphaeria canker, both of which are more common in Georgia's humid, high-density plantings, and it can suffer in prolonged drought or poorly drained clay. We still recommend it for customers who specifically want its softer texture and taller ceiling, planted with good air circulation, full sun, and spacing that reduces disease pressure. Its rapid growth means a young screen can reach usable privacy height in 3 to 5 years, faster than almost any broadleaf evergreen.
plantingTips: Give Leyland Cypress full sun and excellent drainage; in Gwinnett clay, plant on a slight mound and avoid low, wet spots where canker takes hold. Space trees 8-10 feet apart to maintain airflow and reduce disease pressure, wider than you would space Green Giant Arborvitae. Water deeply during the first two summers and avoid overhead irrigation that keeps foliage wet, which encourages fungal issues in our humid climate.
fastFacts: Mature height: 40-60 ft, width 15-20 ft — needs a large lot
Very fast growth: 3-4 ft per year
More susceptible to canker disease than Green Giant Arborvitae
Full sun and good drainage reduce disease risk
Deer resistant, soft blue-green feathery foliage
Recommended spacing: 8-10 ft apart for airflow

faqs.question: Why do Leyland Cypress trees die suddenly?
faqs.answer: Leyland Cypress often dies from Seiridium or Botryosphaeria canker, fungal diseases that thrive in crowded plantings with poor air circulation and stressed, drought-weakened trees. In Georgia's humid summers, planting too closely together or in poorly drained clay is the most common cause of sudden decline.

faqs.question: How far apart should Leyland Cypress be planted?
faqs.answer: Space Leyland Cypress 8 to 10 feet apart for a privacy screen to allow adequate air circulation, which significantly reduces canker disease risk. Planting closer together may look fuller sooner but increases the chance of losing trees to fungal disease within 5-10 years.

faqs.question: Is Leyland Cypress a good choice for Georgia yards?
faqs.answer: Leyland Cypress works well on large Georgia properties with full sun and good drainage, offering very fast growth to 40-60 feet. For smaller lots or heavier clay with drainage concerns, Green Giant Arborvitae is generally a more disease-resistant alternative.

name: Wax Myrtle
water: Low to Moderate — drought tolerant once established
bloomSeason: Spring (inconspicuous, followed by fall/winter berries on female plants)
description: Southern Wax Myrtle (Morella cerifera) is a native Georgia evergreen shrub that grows quickly to 15-20 feet, forming a loose, multi-stemmed screen with aromatic, olive-green leaves that release a spicy fragrance when crushed. As a Piedmont and Coastal Plain native, it is naturally adapted to Gwinnett County's clay soils, summer humidity, and periodic drought, requiring no soil amendment or special care once established. It tolerates wet spots and dry spots equally well, a rare trait among screening plants, and thrives in poor soil where less adaptable shrubs struggle. Female plants produce small blue-gray berries in fall and winter that are an important food source for songbirds, particularly migrating yellow-rumped warblers. Because it grows fast and takes hard pruning well, Wax Myrtle is popular as an informal, lower-maintenance alternative to Leyland Cypress for customers who want a native, wildlife-friendly screen rather than a manicured formal hedge. It is not reliably deer-browsed thanks to its aromatic foliage.
plantingTips: Wax Myrtle adapts to nearly any Gwinnett County soil, from wet clay drainage swales to dry sandy slopes, and needs no amendment at planting. Space plants 6-8 feet apart for a naturalistic screen, or prune annually to maintain a more formal hedge shape. Water weekly the first season; afterward it is drought tolerant and rarely needs supplemental irrigation except in extreme heat.
fastFacts: Georgia native evergreen shrub/small tree
Mature height: 15-20 ft, width 10-15 ft
Fast growth: 3-4 ft per year
Extremely adaptable — tolerates wet or dry soil
Aromatic foliage deters deer browsing
Female plants produce berries that feed songbirds

faqs.question: Is Wax Myrtle native to Georgia?
faqs.answer: Yes, Wax Myrtle (Morella cerifera) is native throughout Georgia's Piedmont and Coastal Plain regions, including Gwinnett County. It is naturally adapted to local clay soils and climate, requiring no soil amendment and tolerating both wet and dry planting sites better than most screening shrubs.

faqs.question: Does Wax Myrtle work in wet areas?
faqs.answer: Yes, Wax Myrtle tolerates poorly drained, seasonally wet soil better than almost any other privacy shrub, making it ideal for low spots or drainage swales in Georgia yards. It also tolerates dry, sandy conditions, giving it unusual flexibility across varying soil types on one property.

faqs.question: Do wax myrtles attract birds?
faqs.answer: Yes, female Wax Myrtle shrubs produce small waxy blue-gray berries in fall and winter that are a favorite food of yellow-rumped warblers and other songbirds. Planting both male and female specimens ensures reliable berry production for wildlife value.

name: Skip Laurel
water: Moderate — weekly until established
description: Skip Laurel (Prunus laurocerasus 'Schipkaensis') is a dense, broadleaf evergreen shrub prized for its glossy dark green foliage and reliable performance in the part shade found under mature Georgia oaks and pines, where sun-hungry conifers like arborvitae struggle. It grows to 10-15 feet tall and 6-10 feet wide at a moderate pace, forming a lush, formal screen that responds well to shearing if a tighter hedge is desired. Skip Laurel is more shade tolerant than Nellie R. Stevens Holly or Leyland Cypress, making it the preferred screening choice for shaded Lawrenceville lots and wooded subdivisions where the property line sits beneath a tree canopy. Fragrant white flower spikes appear in spring, followed by small dark berries. It is not deer resistant and can suffer leaf spot disease in poorly drained, overly wet clay, so a well-drained planting site is important. Skip Laurel also tolerates urban pollution and compacted soil reasonably well, making it a good fit for tighter residential lots.
plantingTips: Skip Laurel prefers part shade to filtered sun and well-drained soil; in Gwinnett clay, improve drainage by planting high and mulching rather than digging low. Space plants 5-6 feet apart for a solid screen. Water consistently the first year, especially during summer dry spells, and avoid overhead watering late in the day, which promotes shot-hole and leaf spot fungal issues common on cherry laurels in humid Georgia summers.
fastFacts: Mature height: 10-15 ft, width 6-10 ft
More shade tolerant than most screening conifers
Moderate growth: 1-2 ft per year
Glossy dark green evergreen foliage, fragrant spring flowers
Not deer resistant; foliage and seeds are toxic to pets
Prone to leaf spot in poorly drained, overly wet soil

faqs.question: Will Skip Laurel grow in shade?
faqs.answer: Yes, Skip Laurel tolerates part shade better than most screening evergreens, making it a top choice for privacy under mature tree canopy in wooded Georgia lots. It still flowers and fills in well with only 4-6 hours of filtered or morning sun per day.

faqs.question: How far apart should Skip Laurel be planted for a hedge?
faqs.answer: Space Skip Laurel 5 to 6 feet apart on center to form a solid, continuous hedge within a few growing seasons. Tighter spacing of 4 feet fills in faster but increases humidity between plants, raising the risk of leaf spot disease in Georgia's summers.

faqs.question: Is Skip Laurel toxic to dogs?
faqs.answer: Yes, Skip Laurel contains cyanogenic compounds in its leaves and seeds that are toxic to dogs and cats if chewed or ingested in quantity. Keep pets from chewing on fallen leaves or berries, and consult a vet promptly if ingestion is suspected.

name: Oakland Holly
water: Moderate — weekly until established, then drought tolerant
bloomSeason: N/A (small spring flowers, grown for foliage)
description: Oakland Holly (Ilex x attenuata 'Oakland') is a narrower-growing hybrid holly bred for a tighter, more uniform pyramidal shape than older selections like Nellie R. Stevens, reaching 15-20 feet tall but only 8-10 feet wide. That narrower footprint makes it a strong option for Gwinnett County side-yard screens where space is tighter than a backyard property line. Its foliage is smooth-edged with fewer spines than traditional hollies, making maintenance and cleanup easier for homeowners. Growth is moderate to fast at about 2 feet per year, and the plant naturally holds a dense, formal pyramid without heavy shearing. Oakland Holly is heat and humidity tolerant, handles Georgia's clay soil well when drainage is adequate, and shows good resistance to common holly pests. It produces red berries in fall and winter that persist into the season, adding color to an otherwise all-green privacy planting. This holly is an increasingly popular alternative in newer Lawrenceville developments where landscape plans call for a uniform, formal evergreen screen with a narrower mature width than classic large hollies.
plantingTips: Plant Oakland Holly in full sun to part shade with well-drained soil; as with other hollies in Georgia clay, set the root ball slightly high and mulch well rather than planting in a deep hole. Space plants 5-7 feet apart for a tight, uniform screen given its narrower mature width. Water deeply twice weekly through the first summer, then taper to occasional deep watering during drought.
fastFacts: Mature height: 15-20 ft, width only 8-10 ft — narrower than most hollies
Fewer spines than traditional holly cultivars, easier to maintain
Growth rate: about 2 ft per year
Naturally dense pyramidal form, needs minimal shearing
Deer resistant and heat/humidity tolerant
Berries persist into winter for color and bird food

faqs.question: How wide does Oakland Holly grow?
faqs.answer: Oakland Holly matures to only 8-10 feet wide while reaching 15-20 feet tall, noticeably narrower than Nellie R. Stevens Holly. This makes it well suited to tighter side-yard screens and narrow lot lines common in newer Gwinnett County subdivisions.

faqs.question: Does Oakland Holly need pruning?
faqs.answer: Oakland Holly naturally forms a dense, uniform pyramid and needs little pruning to maintain its shape, unlike faster or looser-growing screening plants. Occasional light shaping after the spring growth flush keeps the form tidy but is optional rather than required.

name: Needlepoint Holly
water: Low to Moderate — drought tolerant once established
bloomSeason: N/A (small spring flowers, grown for foliage)
description: Needlepoint Holly (Ilex cornuta 'Needlepoint') is a refined Chinese Holly selection with distinctive single-spined, glossy dark-green leaves that curve downward, giving the foliage a soft, elegant look despite the plant's toughness. It grows to a compact 8-10 feet tall and 5-6 feet wide, smaller than most privacy hollies, which makes it equally useful as a foundation shrub, low screen, or clipped hedge in Lawrenceville landscapes. It is self-fruiting like Nellie R. Stevens, setting heavy crops of bright red berries without a male pollinator, and those berries persist through winter, feeding birds when other food sources are scarce. Needlepoint Holly tolerates Georgia's clay soil, summer heat, and humidity with few disease problems, and once established it is notably drought tolerant, requiring far less supplemental water than azaleas or hydrangeas planted nearby. Its smaller mature size and formal texture make it a favorite for framing entryways and foundation plantings across Gwinnett County, in addition to its use as a compact screening plant.
plantingTips: Plant in full sun to part shade with well-drained soil, setting the top of the root ball slightly above grade in Georgia clay. Space plants 3-4 feet apart for a tight foundation hedge, or 5 feet apart for a taller screen. Water weekly the first growing season; established plants tolerate drought well and need supplemental water only during extended dry spells.
fastFacts: Compact mature size: 8-10 ft tall, 5-6 ft wide
Self-fruiting — produces red berries without a male holly
Single-spined leaves, softer look than traditional holly
Drought tolerant once established
Deer resistant, low-maintenance evergreen
Popular as both a foundation shrub and low privacy hedge

faqs.question: How big does Needlepoint Holly get?
faqs.answer: Needlepoint Holly matures to a compact 8-10 feet tall and 5-6 feet wide, considerably smaller than large screening hollies like Nellie R. Stevens. This makes it ideal for foundation plantings, low hedges, or narrower privacy screens in smaller Georgia yards.

faqs.question: Does Needlepoint Holly need a male plant for berries?
faqs.answer: No, Needlepoint Holly is self-fruiting and reliably produces bright red winter berries without a separate male pollinator nearby. This is one of the main reasons it's favored for consistent winter color in Georgia Favorites plantings across Gwinnett County.

name: Burford Holly
water: Low — very drought tolerant once established
bloomSeason: N/A (small spring flowers, grown for foliage)
description: Burford Holly (Ilex cornuta 'Burfordii') is a large, tough evergreen shrub with distinctive glossy leaves that each carry a single spine at the tip rather than the multiple spines of American Holly, and it has been a Southern landscape staple for generations because of its near-indestructible nature. It reaches 15-20 feet tall and 10-15 feet wide if left unpruned, though it is commonly sheared into a formal hedge at 6-10 feet. Burford Holly is self-fruiting and loads up with large red berries every fall, among the showiest of any holly. It is exceptionally drought tolerant once established and shrugs off Georgia's compacted clay, summer heat, and poor soil better than almost any other screening plant we carry, thriving in conditions that would stress hydrangeas or azaleas. Its dense, thorny-tipped foliage also makes it an effective deterrent hedge along property lines where an extra layer of security-conscious screening is wanted, in addition to its straightforward privacy value.
plantingTips: Burford Holly tolerates a wide range of Georgia soils, including compacted clay and dry, sunny slopes where other shrubs fail. Plant with the root ball slightly above grade, space 6-8 feet apart for a screen or 4-5 feet for a formal hedge, and water weekly the first season. Once established it needs little irrigation and tolerates hard pruning well if size control is needed.
fastFacts: Mature height: 15-20 ft, width 10-15 ft if unpruned
Extremely drought tolerant once established
Self-fruiting with heavy fall berry crops
Single spine per leaf tip, unlike multi-spined hollies
Tolerates poor, compacted clay soil better than most shrubs
Deer resistant and long-lived Southern landscape classic

faqs.question: How big does Burford Holly get if not pruned?
faqs.answer: Left unpruned, Burford Holly grows into a large shrub or small tree 15-20 feet tall and 10-15 feet wide. Most Georgia homeowners maintain it as a sheared hedge at 6-10 feet, but it can be allowed to reach full size as a substantial privacy screen or specimen.

faqs.question: Is Burford Holly drought tolerant?
faqs.answer: Yes, Burford Holly is one of the most drought-tolerant screening shrubs available, thriving in Georgia's hot, dry summer stretches once its root system is established, usually after the first full year in the ground. It requires far less irrigation than hydrangeas or azaleas planted nearby.

name: Dwarf Burford Holly
water: Low — very drought tolerant once established
bloomSeason: N/A (small spring flowers, grown for foliage)
description: Dwarf Burford Holly (Ilex cornuta 'Burfordii Nana') is a compact sport of standard Burford Holly, growing to just 6-8 feet tall and 5-6 feet wide, which makes it far better suited to foundation plantings, low hedges, and smaller Gwinnett County lots than its full-size parent. It keeps the same glossy, single-spined leaves and heavy crop of red fall berries, produced without needing a male pollinator, but stays proportional to a one-story house foundation or a smaller privacy screen along a side yard. Like standard Burford Holly, it is exceptionally tough, tolerating compacted clay, drought, heat, and neglect better than almost any broadleaf evergreen sold in the Atlanta metro. It responds well to shearing for a formal hedge or can be left loosely pruned for a fuller, more natural mounded form. Because it stays smaller without constant pruning, it is one of the lowest-maintenance options for homeowners who want a holly's toughness and berries without the eventual size of standard Burford Holly.
plantingTips: Dwarf Burford Holly tolerates nearly any well-drained Georgia soil, including clay and compacted subdivision fill dirt. Space plants 3-4 feet apart for a hedge or foundation row. Water weekly for the first growing season; afterward it needs supplemental water only during extended drought. Prune after berries fade in late winter if a tighter shape is desired. Once established in a Gwinnett County landscape, it needs only occasional deep watering during dry stretches rather than a regular irrigation schedule.
fastFacts: Compact form: 6-8 ft tall, 5-6 ft wide
Dwarf sport of standard Burford Holly
Self-fruiting with reliable red winter berries
Extremely drought and heat tolerant
Deer resistant, low-maintenance evergreen
Ideal for foundation plantings and smaller lots

faqs.question: What is the difference between Burford Holly and Dwarf Burford Holly?
faqs.answer: Dwarf Burford Holly stays 6-8 feet tall and 5-6 feet wide, roughly half the size of standard Burford Holly, which reaches 15-20 feet. Both share the same glossy foliage, drought tolerance, and self-fruiting red berries, but the dwarf form suits foundation plantings and smaller yards better.

faqs.question: Is Dwarf Burford Holly deer resistant?
faqs.answer: Yes, Dwarf Burford Holly is considered deer resistant, making it a reliable choice for Gwinnett County properties bordering wooded areas with regular deer traffic. As with any "deer resistant" plant, hungry deer in a hard winter may still sample new growth occasionally, but damage is typically minimal.

name: American Holly
water: Moderate until established, then drought tolerant
bloomSeason: N/A (small spring flowers; berries need male and female plants)
description: American Holly (Ilex opaca) is the native evergreen holly of the eastern United States, a slow-growing but long-lived tree reaching 30-50 feet with the classic spiny, dull-green leaves and red winter berries associated with the species. Unlike self-fruiting hybrid hollies such as Nellie R. Stevens, American Holly is dioecious, meaning separate male and female plants are required for the females to set berries, so at least one male should be planted within pollinating range. As a true Georgia native, it is exceptionally well adapted to Piedmont clay soils, tolerates both sun and considerable shade beneath a taller canopy, and supports native wildlife, including berries that feed cedar waxwings and other birds through winter. Growth is slow at about 1 foot per year, so it is best chosen by customers planning a long-term screen or specimen tree rather than a quick fix. Its dense, pyramidal form and rough, spiny leaves also make it useful as a barrier planting, and its wood and wide native range have long made it a traditional Southern landscape tree.
plantingTips: American Holly tolerates Georgia's clay soil and both sun and shade, making it flexible for wooded or open Gwinnett County lots. Plant at least one male cultivar for every 8-10 female plants to ensure berry production. Because growth is slow, choose a larger container size if a faster-established screen is the goal, and mulch well to conserve moisture while the extensive root system develops.
fastFacts: Georgia native evergreen tree, mature height 30-50 ft
Slow growth: about 1 ft per year
Dioecious — needs both male and female plants for berries
Tolerates full sun to significant shade
Deer resistant, supports native bird species
Long-lived, traditional Southern holiday holly

faqs.question: Do you need a male and female American Holly to get berries?
faqs.answer: Yes, American Holly is dioecious, so a female plant only produces berries if a male American Holly (or compatible male Ilex opaca cultivar) is growing within bee-pollinating range, typically within a few hundred feet. Without a male nearby, female plants will flower but set no berries.

faqs.question: How fast does American Holly grow?
faqs.answer: American Holly grows slowly, about 1 foot per year, much slower than hybrid hollies like Nellie R. Stevens. Because of this, we recommend starting with a larger container size if you want a mature-looking screen or specimen within a shorter timeframe.

name: Foster Holly
water: Moderate — weekly until established, then drought tolerant
bloomSeason: N/A (small spring flowers, grown for foliage)
description: Foster Holly (Ilex x attenuata 'Fosteri') is a naturally occurring hybrid between American Holly and Dahoon Holly, combining a graceful, narrow pyramidal form with fine-textured, small spiny leaves that give it a softer, more refined look than either parent species. It grows at a moderate pace to 20-25 feet tall and only 10-12 feet wide, making it a good middle-ground option between the wide-spreading Burford Holly and the very narrow Emerald Green Arborvitae for Lawrenceville property lines. Foster Holly produces abundant small red berries in fall that persist well into winter and are a favorite of songbirds, and because it sets fruit reliably it is popular as both a screening plant and a specimen tree near entrances. It adapts well to Georgia's clay soils and tolerates both full sun and part shade, though foliage density and berry production are best in more sun. Its finer-textured leaves and elegant pyramidal habit make it a slightly more formal-looking alternative to bulkier hollies for foundation and screening use.
plantingTips: Plant Foster Holly in full sun to part shade with well-drained soil; in Georgia clay, set the root ball slightly high and mulch generously. Space plants 6-8 feet apart for a screen. Water deeply twice a week during the first growing season, then reduce frequency as the root system establishes. Light pruning after berry season maintains its naturally narrow pyramidal form.
fastFacts: Mature height: 20-25 ft, width 10-12 ft
Fine-textured, small spiny leaves — softer look than Burford Holly
Natural hybrid of American and Dahoon Holly
Heavy, long-lasting red berry crop
Deer resistant, tolerates sun to part shade
Elegant narrow pyramidal form, good for specimen or screen use

faqs.question: How is Foster Holly different from American Holly?
faqs.answer: Foster Holly is a naturally occurring hybrid with finer, smaller leaves and a narrower, more formal pyramidal shape than American Holly, and it grows somewhat faster. Both are excellent for Georgia landscapes, but Foster Holly's more refined texture suits entrance plantings and tighter screens especially well.

faqs.question: Is Foster Holly deer resistant?
faqs.answer: Yes, Foster Holly is considered deer resistant, making it a reliable choice for Gwinnett County properties bordering wooded areas with regular deer traffic. As with any "deer resistant" plant, hungry deer in a hard winter may still sample new growth occasionally, but damage is typically minimal.

name: Yoshino Cryptomeria
water: Moderate until established, then drought tolerant
description: Yoshino Cryptomeria (Cryptomeria japonica 'Yoshino') is a fast-growing Japanese cedar with soft, feathery blue-green foliage that takes on a slight bronze cast in winter, reaching 30-40 feet tall and 15-20 feet wide in a dense pyramidal form. It grows 2-3 feet per year, filling in a large-scale privacy screen faster than most broadleaf evergreens, and it is notably more disease resistant than Leyland Cypress, which makes it an increasingly popular substitute for customers who want a tall conifer screen without the canker risk. Yoshino Cryptomeria handles Georgia's clay soil and humid summers well once established, and its soft texture and graceful, slightly drooping branch tips give it a less formal, more naturalistic look than arborvitae. It is deer resistant and generally pest-free in our region. Because of its eventual height and width, it works best on larger properties or along back property lines with 15-20 feet of clearance, rather than tight side yards where a narrower conifer like Emerald Green Arborvitae would be more appropriate.
plantingTips: Plant Yoshino Cryptomeria in full sun to part shade with well-drained soil; it tolerates Georgia clay reasonably well but benefits from a slightly raised planting area in heavier ground. Space trees 10-12 feet apart for a naturalistic screen. Water deeply weekly for the first two growing seasons. Minimal pruning is needed; its habit is naturally dense and pyramidal. Once established in a Gwinnett County landscape, it needs only occasional deep watering during dry stretches rather than a regular irrigation schedule.

faqs.question: Is Yoshino Cryptomeria better than Leyland Cypress?
faqs.answer: Yoshino Cryptomeria grows nearly as fast as Leyland Cypress but shows significantly better resistance to the canker diseases that commonly kill Leyland Cypress in Georgia's humid climate. For customers wanting a tall, fast conifer screen with fewer disease concerns, Yoshino Cryptomeria is often the better long-term choice.

faqs.question: Is Yoshino Cryptomeria deer resistant?
faqs.answer: Yes, Yoshino Cryptomeria is considered deer resistant, making it a reliable choice for Gwinnett County properties bordering wooded areas with regular deer traffic. As with any "deer resistant" plant, hungry deer in a hard winter may still sample new growth occasionally, but damage is typically minimal.

name: Radicans Cryptomeria
water: Moderate until established, then drought tolerant
description: Radicans Cryptomeria (Cryptomeria japonica 'Radicans') is a denser, more compact Japanese cedar cultivar than Yoshino, reaching 20-30 feet tall and 10-15 feet wide with tighter, richer green foliage that holds its color through winter without the bronze cast seen in Yoshino Cryptomeria. It grows fast at 2-3 feet per year and forms a fuller, more solid screen from ground to top, which makes it a popular choice for Gwinnett County homeowners who want a conifer privacy screen with dense coverage low to the ground rather than the slightly looser habit of Yoshino. Like other cryptomeria, it resists the canker diseases that affect Leyland Cypress and performs reliably in Georgia's clay soil and humid summers once its root system is established. Its fine, soft texture makes it pleasant near patios and walkways where people brush against the foliage, unlike spinier hollies. Radicans Cryptomeria is a strong middle-ground choice between the very fast, very large Leyland Cypress and the slower, narrower Emerald Green Arborvitae.
plantingTips: Plant in full sun to part shade with good drainage; mound Georgia clay planting sites slightly to avoid standing water. Space plants 8-10 feet apart for a dense screen from top to bottom. Water deeply weekly through the first two summers. Little pruning is required since Radicans naturally holds a tight, full form. Once established in a Gwinnett County landscape, it needs only occasional deep watering during dry stretches rather than a regular irrigation schedule.

faqs.question: What is the difference between Radicans and Yoshino Cryptomeria?
faqs.answer: Radicans Cryptomeria is denser and more compact (20-30 ft) with tighter foliage that holds its green color better in winter, while Yoshino grows slightly larger (30-40 ft) with a looser habit and mild winter bronzing. Radicans fills in low to the ground more solidly, making it better for tighter screens.

faqs.question: Is Radicans Cryptomeria deer resistant?
faqs.answer: Yes, Radicans Cryptomeria is considered deer resistant, making it a reliable choice for Gwinnett County properties bordering wooded areas with regular deer traffic. As with any "deer resistant" plant, hungry deer in a hard winter may still sample new growth occasionally, but damage is typically minimal.

name: Little Gem Magnolia
water: Moderate until established, then drought tolerant
bloomSeason: Late Spring through Summer (repeat, sporadic into fall)
description: Little Gem Magnolia (Magnolia grandiflora 'Little Gem') is a dwarf cultivar of the native Southern Magnolia, bred to stay a manageable 20-25 feet tall and 10-15 feet wide instead of the 60-80 feet a standard Southern Magnolia reaches, while keeping the same glossy evergreen leaves with rusty-brown undersides and large, fragrant creamy-white flowers. It blooms first in late spring and continues sporadically through summer and into fall, giving it a far longer bloom season than most flowering trees in a Georgia landscape. Because it branches densely from near ground level, it doubles as an excellent evergreen privacy screen as well as a specimen tree, and Lawrenceville homeowners frequently plant a row along a property line to get both screening and season-long fragrant blooms. As a native species selection, it is well adapted to Piedmont clay and regional humidity, and it is more tolerant of a range of soil conditions than many ornamental trees. Its dense form and moderate growth rate of 1-2 feet per year make it slower to establish than fast conifers but longer-lived and lower-maintenance once mature.
plantingTips: Plant Little Gem Magnolia in full sun to part shade in well-drained soil, amending heavy Georgia clay minimally and mulching well to retain moisture, since magnolias have shallow, wide-spreading roots. Space plants 8-10 feet apart for a screen, or give a single specimen 15 feet of clearance. Water deeply and regularly for the first two years while the root system establishes; avoid disturbing soil near the trunk once planted.

faqs.question: How big does Little Gem Magnolia get?
faqs.answer: Little Gem Magnolia matures to 20-25 feet tall and 10-15 feet wide, far smaller than a standard Southern Magnolia's 60-80 foot height. This compact size makes it practical as a flowering privacy screen or specimen tree on typical Lawrenceville residential lots.

faqs.question: How long does Little Gem Magnolia bloom?
faqs.answer: Little Gem Magnolia produces its main flush of large, fragrant white blooms in late spring, then continues flowering sporadically through summer and into early fall. This repeat-blooming habit gives it a much longer flowering season than most Southern trees.

name: Bracken's Brown Beauty Magnolia
water: Moderate until established, then drought tolerant
description: Bracken's Brown Beauty Magnolia (Magnolia grandiflora 'Bracken's Brown Beauty') is a Southern Magnolia cultivar prized for its more compact, denser form than the species type, reaching 30-40 feet tall and 15-20 feet wide, and for the striking cinnamon-brown felted undersides of its glossy evergreen leaves, which show attractively whenever wind lifts the foliage. It produces large, fragrant creamy-white blooms from late spring through summer and is considered more cold hardy and more tolerant of heavy soils than many other magnolia selections, an advantage in Gwinnett County's clay-heavy Piedmont ground. Its denser branching habit compared to standard Southern Magnolia makes it a good screening tree as well as a specimen, and it holds foliage lower to the ground than many magnolias, adding privacy value without pruning. As a native species selection, it requires little intervention once established and tolerates both drought and Georgia's humid summers well. This is one of the most reliable broadleaf evergreens for a combined screening-and-flowering tree in Zone 8a landscapes.
plantingTips: Plant in full sun to part shade in well-drained soil; magnolias have shallow, wide roots so avoid deep planting or heavy soil disturbance nearby. Mulch generously to retain moisture in Georgia's clay. Space trees 10-12 feet apart for screening use, or allow 15-20 feet for a single specimen. Water deeply and regularly for the first two years to establish a strong root system.

faqs.question: How is Bracken's Brown Beauty different from a standard Southern Magnolia?
faqs.answer: Bracken's Brown Beauty stays more compact at 30-40 feet versus 60-80 feet for standard Southern Magnolia, with denser branching and distinctive cinnamon-brown leaf undersides. It is also noted for better cold hardiness and heavy-soil tolerance, making it a strong fit for Georgia's clay-based Piedmont landscapes.

faqs.question: Is Bracken's Brown Beauty Magnolia native to Georgia?
faqs.answer: Yes, Bracken's Brown Beauty Magnolia is native to Georgia and the Southeastern United States, which makes it naturally well adapted to the region's clay soils, summer humidity, and Zone 8a climate. Native status generally means less supplemental water and fertilizer are needed once the plant is established in a Lawrenceville landscape.

name: Tea Olive (Fragrant Osmanthus)
water: Moderate — weekly until established, then drought tolerant
bloomSeason: Fall (with light sporadic bloom in spring)
description: Tea Olive (Osmanthus fragrans) is grown less for showy flowers, its small white blooms are easy to overlook, and more for arguably the most fragrant flower of any Southern landscape shrub, filling an entire yard with an apricot-like sweetness every fall when it blooms. It grows into a dense, glossy-leaved evergreen 15-20 feet tall and 8-12 feet wide, functioning as an effective privacy screen while doubling as a fragrance plant near patios, porches, and windows where its scent can be enjoyed. Gwinnett County gardeners often plant it close to outdoor living spaces specifically for the fall fragrance, then let it also serve screening duty along a fence or property line. It tolerates Georgia's clay soil and summer humidity well and is generally trouble-free once established, with few pest or disease issues. Growth is moderate, roughly 1-2 feet per year, making it slower to fill in than a conifer but exceptionally long-lived and low-maintenance, tolerating both sun and considerable shade beneath taller trees.
plantingTips: Plant Tea Olive in full sun to part shade in well-drained soil, siting it near a patio, walkway, or window where its fall fragrance can be appreciated. Space plants 6-8 feet apart for screening. Water weekly the first season; established plants are moderately drought tolerant. It tolerates pruning well if a more formal hedge shape is preferred over its natural rounded form.

faqs.question: When does Tea Olive bloom?
faqs.answer: Tea Olive blooms primarily in fall, typically September through November in Georgia, producing small white flowers with an intensely sweet, apricot-like fragrance that can perfume an entire yard. Some plants also produce lighter, sporadic blooms in spring.

faqs.question: Is Tea Olive good for privacy?
faqs.answer: Yes, Tea Olive grows into a dense evergreen screen 15-20 feet tall and 8-12 feet wide, making it effective for privacy while also providing intensely fragrant fall flowers, a dual benefit few other screening plants offer for Georgia landscapes.

name: Carolina Cherry Laurel
water: Low to Moderate — drought tolerant once established
description: Carolina Cherry Laurel (Prunus caroliniana) is a fast-growing native evergreen tree that forms a dense screen of glossy dark-green leaves, reaching 20-25 feet tall and 10-15 feet wide, and is one of the quickest broadleaf evergreens available for Georgia privacy plantings, growing 2-3 feet per year once established. Small white flowers appear in early spring, followed by small black fruit that birds readily eat. As a Southeastern native, it is naturally suited to Gwinnett County's clay soils and climate, tolerating both drought and periods of wet weather better than many non-native screening shrubs, and it handles heat and humidity without issue. It responds very well to shearing and is commonly maintained as a formal hedge as well as left to grow into a small tree for a taller screen. All parts of the plant, leaves, bark, and seeds, contain cyanogenic compounds and are toxic if ingested, so it should be sited away from areas where pets or children might chew on fallen leaves or fruit.
plantingTips: Carolina Cherry Laurel adapts to a wide range of Georgia soils including clay, and tolerates both sun and part shade. Space plants 6-8 feet apart for a fast-filling screen, or 4-5 feet for a tight formal hedge. Water weekly the first season; it becomes drought tolerant once established. Prune after spring flowering if a more formal shape is desired; avoid planting where pets can access dropped leaves or fruit.

faqs.question: Is Carolina Cherry Laurel fast growing?
faqs.answer: Yes, Carolina Cherry Laurel grows 2-3 feet per year once established, making it one of the faster native evergreen options for privacy screening in Georgia. A young planting can form a solid screen within 3-4 years under good growing conditions.

faqs.question: Is Carolina Cherry Laurel poisonous?
faqs.answer: Yes, all parts of Carolina Cherry Laurel, including leaves, bark, and seeds, contain cyanogenic compounds that are toxic if ingested by pets, livestock, or humans. Plant it away from areas where pets graze on fallen foliage, and supervise children around the fruit.

name: Eastern Red Cedar
water: Low — very drought tolerant once established
bloomSeason: N/A (evergreen conifer; female trees produce blue-gray berry cones)
description: Eastern Red Cedar (Juniperus virginiana) is a native evergreen conifer found throughout Georgia's old fields and fence rows, valued in the landscape for its columnar to pyramidal form, aromatic reddish wood, and exceptional toughness in poor, dry, rocky soil where few other screening plants survive. It reaches 30-40 feet tall and 8-15 feet wide, with fine scale-like blue-green foliage that takes on a purplish-bronze cast in winter. Female trees produce small blue-gray berry-like cones that are an important winter food source for cedar waxwings, and the tree's common name comes directly from that bird. As a true native, it thrives in Gwinnett County's clay soil and tolerates drought, heat, and poor fertility better than nearly any other privacy conifer, requiring essentially no maintenance once established. It does host cedar-apple rust, a fungal disease that also affects apple trees, so it is best not planted within a few hundred feet of an orchard planting. Its wide native range, from Zone 7a into warmer Zone 9b areas, reflects its broad adaptability.
plantingTips: Eastern Red Cedar thrives in full sun and tolerates poor, dry, rocky, or clay soils better than almost any other evergreen. Space plants 8-10 feet apart for a naturalistic screen. Water weekly the first season; afterward it is highly drought tolerant and needs no supplemental irrigation. Avoid planting near apple or crabapple trees due to shared susceptibility to cedar-apple rust.

faqs.question: Should I plant Eastern Red Cedar near apple trees?
faqs.answer: No, Eastern Red Cedar hosts cedar-apple rust, a fungal disease that alternates between cedar and apple trees to complete its life cycle, and can significantly damage apple foliage and fruit. Keep red cedars at least a few hundred feet from any apple or crabapple plantings when possible.

faqs.question: Is Eastern Red Cedar good for poor soil?
faqs.answer: Yes, Eastern Red Cedar is one of the most soil-adaptable native conifers, thriving in poor, dry, rocky, or compacted clay where many other screening plants struggle. This makes it a practical choice for difficult sites across Gwinnett County where soil quality is a concern.

name: Clumping Bamboo
water: Moderate — regular water for lush growth
bloomSeason: N/A (rarely flowers; grown for foliage and canes)
description: Clumping Bamboo (Fargesia and Bambusa selections sold as non-invasive clumping types) provides the fast, dense, tropical-textured screen homeowners picture when they think of bamboo, without the aggressively spreading rhizomes of running bamboo species that can escape into neighboring yards. It grows in tight, expanding clumps rather than sending runners, reaching 12-20 feet tall with slender canes and fine evergreen foliage that moves attractively in the wind. Growth is fast, adding 3-6 feet per year in a establishing clump, and a planted row fills in to a solid privacy screen faster than most woody shrubs. Clumping bamboo tolerates Georgia's clay soil provided drainage is adequate and appreciates consistent moisture and mulch, since it is not as drought tolerant as native screening shrubs. It is an excellent choice for a distinctive, fast, evergreen screen along a fence line or pool area where a tropical look is wanted, and because it stays in a slowly widening clump rather than spreading, it is far more manageable in a residential Lawrenceville yard than running bamboo species.
plantingTips: Plant clumping bamboo in full sun to part shade in well-drained, consistently moist soil; amend heavy Georgia clay with compost at planting and mulch thickly to retain moisture. Space clumps 4-6 feet apart for a continuous screen, allowing room for the clump to widen over years. Water regularly, especially the first two growing seasons, and fertilize in spring for lush cane and foliage growth.

faqs.question: Is clumping bamboo invasive?
faqs.answer: No, clumping bamboo grows in tight, slowly expanding clumps rather than sending out aggressive underground runners like running bamboo species. It stays where planted and is considered a manageable, non-invasive option for privacy screening in residential Georgia landscapes.

faqs.question: How much water does clumping bamboo need?
faqs.answer: Clumping bamboo needs more consistent moisture than most privacy shrubs, especially during its first two establishing seasons and throughout hot Georgia summers. Regular deep watering and a thick mulch layer keep the foliage lush and support the 3-6 feet of annual growth it's known for.

name: Encore Azalea
water: Moderate — regular water, avoid drought stress
description: Encore Azalea is a patented series of repeat-blooming azaleas that flower not only in spring like traditional Southern azaleas, but again in summer and often a third time in fall, thanks to breeding that incorporated a repeat-flowering Asian azalea species. It grows into a rounded shrub 3-4 feet tall and wide, and unlike many older azalea varieties it tolerates more sun, up to 4-6 hours of direct sun actually improves flowering and reblooming, while still handling the part shade found under Georgia's pine and oak canopy. Encore Azaleas need consistently moist, acidic, well-drained soil, which makes bed preparation important in Gwinnett County's clay, since azaleas are shallow-rooted and quickly stressed by both drought and waterlogging. They are available in numerous named colors (Autumn Bonfire, Autumn Twist, and others), all sharing the same repeat-bloom trait. Because they extend the traditional azalea bloom window from a few spring weeks to three seasons of color, Encore Azalea has become one of the most requested flowering shrubs for Lawrenceville landscapes wanting more than a single spring show.
plantingTips: Prepare a bed amended with pine bark fines or compost to improve drainage and acidity in Georgia's clay, since Encore Azaleas need consistently moist but well-drained soil. Plant with the root ball slightly above grade and mulch 2-3 inches deep to conserve moisture and moderate soil temperature. Water deeply twice weekly during summer heat, and avoid deep cultivation near roots, which are shallow and easily damaged.

faqs.question: How many times a year does Encore Azalea bloom?
faqs.answer: Encore Azalea typically blooms three times a year: a heavy flush in spring, a second bloom in summer, and a third in fall, thanks to breeding with a repeat-flowering azalea species. This gives roughly three seasons of color compared to the single spring bloom of traditional Southern azaleas.

faqs.question: How much sun does Encore Azalea need?
faqs.answer: Encore Azalea performs best with 4-6 hours of direct sun per day, more sun than traditional shade-loving azaleas tolerate, which actually improves its summer and fall reblooming. It also adapts to part shade but may bloom less in deep shade under dense tree canopy.

faqs.question: Is Encore Azalea toxic to dogs?
faqs.answer: Yes, all azaleas, including Encore Azalea, contain grayanotoxins that are toxic to dogs, cats, and humans if leaves or flowers are ingested, potentially causing vomiting, drooling, and cardiac symptoms. Keep pets from grazing on azalea foliage and seek veterinary care if ingestion is suspected.

name: Traditional Southern Azalea
water: Moderate — consistent moisture, avoid drought stress
description: Traditional Southern Azalea refers to the classic evergreen Indica and Kurume azalea hybrids that have defined Southern spring gardens for over a century, producing an overwhelming single flush of blooms in March and April that can nearly hide the foliage under flower color for two to three weeks. Unlike reblooming Encore Azalea, these traditional varieties bloom only once per year but grow larger, often 4-8 feet tall and 4-6 feet wide at maturity, and are prized for their dramatic, dense floral display and their tolerance of the deep, dappled shade found under mature Georgia hardwoods. They require the same acidic, well-drained, evenly moist soil as all azaleas and are shallow rooted, making them sensitive to both drought and compacted clay. Many older Lawrenceville and Gwinnett County neighborhoods still feature decades-old plantings of traditional azaleas that bloom reliably every spring with minimal care. For customers who want the biggest single spring show and don't need repeat blooming, traditional Southern azaleas remain a classic, lower-cost option.
plantingTips: Plant in part shade to filtered light, avoiding hot afternoon sun which stresses traditional azaleas more than Encore types. Amend Georgia clay with pine bark fines for drainage and acidity, set the root ball slightly high, and mulch well. Water consistently through the first two growing seasons; established plantings still benefit from supplemental water during summer dry spells since roots stay shallow and drought-sensitive.

faqs.question: When do traditional azaleas bloom in Georgia?
faqs.answer: Traditional Southern Azaleas bloom once a year, typically in March and April in the Atlanta metro area, producing a dense, dramatic flush of flowers that can last two to three weeks. Unlike Encore Azalea, they do not rebloom later in summer or fall.

faqs.question: Do deer eat Traditional Southern Azalea?
faqs.answer: Yes, Traditional Southern Azalea is not considered deer resistant and can be browsed by deer, especially newly planted specimens. In Gwinnett County areas with heavy deer pressure, fencing or repellent application is worth considering until the plant is well established.

name: Limelight Hydrangea
water: Moderate to High — consistent moisture, especially in summer
description: Limelight Hydrangea (Hydrangea paniculata 'Limelight') is a panicle hydrangea that produces large, cone-shaped flower clusters starting lime-green in mid-summer and aging through creamy white to deep pink-blush by fall, giving it multiple seasons of color from a single bloom cycle. Unlike bigleaf hydrangeas such as Endless Summer, Limelight blooms on new wood, so late-winter pruning does not remove the coming season's flower buds, and its flower color is not affected by soil pH, meaning it stays reliably green-to-white rather than shifting blue or pink like mophead types. It grows into a large, upright shrub 6-8 feet tall and wide and tolerates significantly more sun than bigleaf hydrangeas, handling Georgia's intense summer sun as long as soil moisture is adequate. This sun tolerance and its more predictable bloom make Limelight one of the most reliable hydrangeas for Gwinnett County landscapes, especially in spots too sunny for Endless Summer or Oakleaf Hydrangea. Its sturdy stems hold the heavy flower heads upright better than many panicle hydrangea cultivars.
plantingTips: Plant Limelight Hydrangea in full sun to part shade in well-drained soil amended with compost; it tolerates more sun than other hydrangeas but needs consistent moisture, especially during Georgia's hot, humid summers. Mulch well to conserve soil moisture. Prune in late winter before new growth emerges, since it blooms on new wood; this is the one hydrangea type where hard pruning does not sacrifice the current season's flowers.

faqs.question: Does Limelight Hydrangea bloom on old or new wood?
faqs.answer: Limelight Hydrangea blooms on new wood, meaning flower buds form on the current season's growth rather than the previous year's stems. This makes it safe to prune hard in late winter without losing that year's blooms, unlike bigleaf hydrangeas such as Endless Summer.

faqs.question: Can Limelight Hydrangea take full sun in Georgia?
faqs.answer: Yes, Limelight Hydrangea tolerates more direct sun than most hydrangeas, including full sun in Georgia if given consistent soil moisture. In hot Gwinnett County summers, afternoon shade helps reduce wilting, but Limelight still outperforms bigleaf types in sunnier planting sites.

name: Endless Summer Hydrangea
water: High — consistent moisture required
bloomSeason: Summer through Fall (reblooms on new and old wood)
description: Endless Summer Hydrangea (Hydrangea macrophylla 'Endless Summer') was the first widely sold bigleaf hydrangea bred to bloom on both old and new wood, meaning that even if late frost or overzealous pruning damages the previous year's stems, the plant still produces flowers on new growth the same season. It grows 3-5 feet tall and wide and produces classic mophead flower clusters whose color shifts with soil pH: blue in acidic soil, pink in more alkaline soil, and often a muddy mauve in Georgia's moderately acidic clay unless amended. Morning sun with afternoon shade is ideal in our climate, since intense afternoon sun causes wilting even with adequate soil moisture. Endless Summer needs consistently moist soil and struggles more than Limelight or Oakleaf Hydrangea during hot, dry stretches, so it's best sited where irrigation is reliable. Because of its extended bloom window and ability to recover from a hard winter, it remains one of the most popular hydrangeas for Lawrenceville shade gardens and foundation plantings that get filtered morning light.
plantingTips: Site Endless Summer Hydrangea where it gets morning sun and afternoon shade; Georgia's intense summer afternoon sun causes excessive wilting even in moist soil. Amend planting soil with compost, and adjust pH with garden sulfur for blue blooms or lime for pink. Water deeply and frequently, especially in summer, since this hydrangea is less drought tolerant than panicle types like Limelight.

faqs.question: How do I make Endless Summer Hydrangea blue?
faqs.answer: To turn Endless Summer Hydrangea blooms blue, lower the soil pH to around 5.0-5.5 using garden sulfur or an aluminum sulfate soil amendment, since blue color develops only when aluminum is available to the plant in acidic soil. Georgia's naturally acidic clay often produces blue-purple blooms without amendment.

faqs.question: Why is my Endless Summer Hydrangea not blooming?
faqs.answer: The most common reasons Endless Summer Hydrangea fails to bloom are late frost damage to old-wood buds, over-pruning in fall or winter, too much shade, or inconsistent watering during bud formation. Because it reblooms on new wood too, most plants still flower some even after a rough winter.

name: Oakleaf Hydrangea
water: Moderate — drought tolerant once established
bloomSeason: Early Summer, with fall foliage color
description: Oakleaf Hydrangea (Hydrangea quercifolia) is native to the Southeastern United States, including Georgia's Piedmont woodlands, and offers more four-season interest than any other hydrangea: large oak-shaped leaves that turn deep burgundy-red in fall, cone-shaped white flower clusters in early summer that age to pink and papery tan, and attractive peeling cinnamon-colored bark visible in winter after leaf drop. It grows 6-8 feet tall and wide and, as a true native, is considerably more drought tolerant once established than non-native hydrangeas like Endless Summer, tolerating both part shade and surprisingly more sun than its bigleaf cousins. Its flower color does not shift with soil pH the way mophead hydrangeas do, so results are more predictable. Because it is native to Georgia woodland edges, it thrives in the dappled shade and clay soil of established Lawrenceville lots without the fussiness of imported hydrangea species, making it a favorite of gardeners wanting a lower-maintenance, wildlife-friendly hydrangea with fall color most hydrangeas lack entirely.
plantingTips: Plant Oakleaf Hydrangea in part shade to morning sun in well-drained soil enriched with compost; it tolerates Georgia clay better than bigleaf hydrangeas once established. Mulch well to retain moisture during establishment, after which it becomes notably drought tolerant. Prune immediately after flowering if shaping is needed, since it blooms on old wood and next year's buds form soon after summer bloom ends.

faqs.question: Is Oakleaf Hydrangea native to Georgia?
faqs.answer: Yes, Oakleaf Hydrangea (Hydrangea quercifolia) is native to the Southeastern United States, including Georgia's Piedmont region, growing naturally in woodland edges and along stream banks. This native origin makes it more drought tolerant and lower-maintenance than non-native hydrangea species once established.

faqs.question: Does Oakleaf Hydrangea have fall color?
faqs.answer: Yes, Oakleaf Hydrangea is the only common hydrangea with significant fall foliage color, turning deep burgundy-red to purple in autumn before dropping to reveal attractive peeling cinnamon bark. This gives it three seasons of interest beyond its early summer white flower clusters.

name: Little Lime Hydrangea
water: Moderate to High — consistent moisture, especially in summer
description: Little Lime Hydrangea (Hydrangea paniculata 'Little Lime') is a dwarf sport of Limelight Hydrangea, delivering the same reliable lime-green-to-pink cone-shaped blooms and new-wood flowering habit on a plant that stays a compact 3-5 feet tall and wide, roughly half the size of full-size Limelight. This makes it a better fit for foundation plantings and smaller Lawrenceville garden beds where the 6-8 foot spread of standard Limelight would be too large. Like all panicle hydrangeas, its flower color is not affected by soil pH, and because it blooms on new wood, late-winter pruning does not sacrifice the coming season's flowers, unlike bigleaf mophead hydrangeas. It tolerates more sun than Endless Summer Hydrangea and holds up better to Georgia's summer heat, provided soil moisture stays consistent. Its sturdy, compact stems support the flower heads well without the flopping some large panicle hydrangeas show after heavy rain, making it a tidy, dependable choice for smaller-scale plantings that still want big hydrangea blooms.
plantingTips: Plant in full sun to part shade in well-drained, compost-enriched soil; provide consistent moisture through Georgia's summer, especially in full sun locations. Space 3-4 feet apart for a mass planting or foundation row. Prune in late winter before new growth if size control is desired, since blooms form on new wood and are not sacrificed by hard pruning. Check soil moisture regularly through the growing season, since Georgia's summer heat can dry out beds faster than expected, and inconsistent moisture is the most common cause of poor performance.

faqs.question: What is the difference between Little Lime and Limelight Hydrangea?
faqs.answer: Little Lime Hydrangea is a dwarf version of Limelight, growing only 3-5 feet tall and wide compared to Limelight's 6-8 feet, while producing the same lime-green-to-pink blooms and new-wood flowering habit. Little Lime suits smaller garden beds and foundation plantings better than full-size Limelight.

faqs.question: Do deer eat Little Lime Hydrangea?
faqs.answer: Yes, Little Lime Hydrangea is not considered deer resistant and can be browsed by deer, especially newly planted specimens. In Gwinnett County areas with heavy deer pressure, fencing or repellent application is worth considering until the plant is well established.

name: Incrediball Hydrangea
water: Moderate to High — consistent moisture, especially in summer
description: Incrediball Hydrangea (Hydrangea arborescens 'Incrediball') is an improved smooth hydrangea bred with much stronger stems than the older 'Annabelle' variety, so its enormous basketball-sized white flower heads, some reaching a foot across, stand upright rather than flopping to the ground after summer thunderstorms, a common frustration Georgia gardeners have with Annabelle Hydrangea. It grows 4-5 feet tall and wide and blooms reliably on new wood, meaning it can be cut back hard each late winter and still produce its full flush of flowers the following summer, making it an especially forgiving hydrangea for gardeners uncertain about pruning timing. It tolerates both full sun and part shade and adapts well to Georgia's clay soil provided moisture stays consistent through the growing season. Unlike bigleaf hydrangeas, Incrediball's white flower color is not influenced by soil pH. Its bold, rounded flower heads make a strong focal statement in mixed shrub borders and pair especially well with panicle hydrangeas for a extended, layered summer bloom display.
plantingTips: Plant in full sun to part shade in compost-enriched, well-drained soil; water deeply and consistently through summer to support the large flower heads. Cut stems back to 12-18 inches in late winter for the strongest new growth and largest blooms, since flowering occurs entirely on new wood. Stake in very windy or exposed sites if flower heads become heavy after rain.

faqs.question: Is Incrediball Hydrangea better than Annabelle?
faqs.answer: Incrediball Hydrangea has significantly stronger, thicker stems than Annabelle Hydrangea, so its large white flower heads stay upright instead of flopping over after rain, a common complaint with Annabelle in Georgia's frequent summer thunderstorms. Both bloom on new wood and can be cut back hard each winter.

faqs.question: Do deer eat Incrediball Hydrangea?

name: Gardenia
water: Moderate — consistent moisture, well-drained soil
description: Gardenia (Gardenia jasminoides) is grown above all for its intensely fragrant, waxy white flowers, considered by many Southern gardeners to be the single most fragrant bloom in the landscape, produced over a long late spring into summer bloom window against glossy, deep-green evergreen foliage. It grows into a rounded shrub 4-6 feet tall and wide and performs best with morning sun and afternoon shade in Georgia's climate, since intense summer afternoon heat can stress the plant and encourage sooty mold from whitefly activity. Gardenias require acidic, well-drained, evenly moist soil, similar to azaleas and camellias, and are prone to yellowing (chlorosis) in Gwinnett County's clay if the soil pH runs too alkaline, which is easily corrected with an acidifying fertilizer. Whitefly and the resulting sooty mold are the most common pest issues in humid Georgia summers, generally manageable with horticultural oil. Because a single flower can perfume an entire porch or patio, gardenias are traditionally planted close to outdoor living spaces, entryways, and bedroom windows across the South.
plantingTips: Plant Gardenia in morning sun with afternoon shade in acidic, well-drained soil amended with pine bark fines or compost. Mulch to retain even moisture, since gardenias dislike both drought and waterlogged clay. Fertilize with an acid-forming, azalea/camellia-type fertilizer in spring. Watch for whitefly on leaf undersides during humid summer months and treat promptly with horticultural oil to prevent sooty mold.

Mature size: 4-6 ft tall and wide

faqs.question: Why are my gardenia leaves turning yellow?
faqs.answer: Yellowing gardenia leaves most often signal iron chlorosis caused by alkaline soil pH, which is common where Georgia clay has been limed or where concrete foundations raise nearby soil pH. Treat with an acid-forming fertilizer formulated for azaleas and gardenias, and confirm with a soil test if yellowing persists.

faqs.question: Is Gardenia safe for pets?
faqs.answer: Yes, Gardenia is generally considered non-toxic and pet safe, unlike many other popular flowering shrubs such as azaleas and hydrangeas. It's a good fragrant flowering option for yards where dogs or cats have access to the planting beds.

name: Frostproof Gardenia
water: Moderate — consistent moisture, well-drained soil
description: Frostproof Gardenia (Gardenia jasminoides 'Frostproof') was selected specifically for improved cold hardiness compared to standard Gardenia jasminoides, an important trait after Georgia occasionally sees hard winter snaps that can damage or kill less hardy gardenia cultivars. It stays more compact than standard gardenia at 3-4 feet tall and wide and produces the same intensely fragrant waxy white flowers over an extended bloom season that stretches from late spring through fall rather than a single flush, giving more months of fragrance in the landscape. Its smaller, denser habit also makes it a better fit for foundation plantings and smaller beds than standard Gardenia. Like other gardenias, it requires acidic, well-drained, consistently moist soil and benefits from morning sun with afternoon shade protection in Georgia's intense summer heat. Frostproof Gardenia's combination of reliable cold hardiness and long bloom season has made it one of the most planted gardenia selections in Gwinnett County landscapes over the past decade.
plantingTips: Plant Frostproof Gardenia in morning sun with afternoon shade in acidic, well-drained soil enriched with pine bark fines. Mulch to maintain even soil moisture. Fertilize with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring to support the extended late-spring-through-fall bloom season. Monitor for whitefly on leaf undersides in humid summer months and treat with horticultural oil as needed. Check soil moisture regularly through the growing season, since Georgia's summer heat can dry out beds faster than expected, and inconsistent moisture is the most common cause of poor performance.

faqs.question: Is Frostproof Gardenia more cold hardy than regular Gardenia?
faqs.answer: Yes, Frostproof Gardenia was specifically selected for improved cold tolerance compared to standard Gardenia jasminoides, making it more reliable through occasional hard winter snaps in Zone 8a Georgia. It still benefits from a protected site during unusually severe cold events.

faqs.question: Do deer eat Frostproof Gardenia?
faqs.answer: Yes, Frostproof Gardenia is not considered deer resistant and can be browsed by deer, especially newly planted specimens. In Gwinnett County areas with heavy deer pressure, fencing or repellent application is worth considering until the plant is well established.

name: August Beauty Gardenia
water: Moderate — consistent moisture, well-drained soil
description: August Beauty Gardenia (Gardenia jasminoides 'August Beauty') is a large-flowered gardenia cultivar bred for one of the longest bloom windows in the species, flowering from late spring all the way through August, well past the single flush many older gardenia types produce. It grows 4-6 feet tall and wide with large, extra-fragrant double white blooms and glossy dark-green foliage. Like all gardenias, it needs acidic, well-drained, consistently moist soil and performs best with morning sun and afternoon shade protection from Georgia's intense summer heat, which can otherwise stress the plant and invite whitefly. Its extended summer bloom season makes it a strong choice for Lawrenceville gardeners who want gardenia fragrance lasting well into the hottest part of the year, rather than concentrated only in a spring flush. As with other gardenias, iron chlorosis (yellowing between leaf veins) can occur in Georgia's often-alkaline urban and new-construction soils and is corrected with acid-forming fertilizer formulated for azaleas and gardenias.
plantingTips: Site August Beauty Gardenia in morning sun with afternoon shade, in acidic, well-drained soil amended with pine bark fines or compost. Mulch to conserve moisture and keep roots cool through Georgia's long summer bloom season. Fertilize with an acid-forming fertilizer in spring and again in early summer to support the extended flowering period. Watch for whitefly and treat with horticultural oil if sooty mold appears.

faqs.question: How long does August Beauty Gardenia bloom?
faqs.answer: August Beauty Gardenia blooms from late spring through August, one of the longest flowering windows of any gardenia cultivar, rather than a single spring flush. This extended bloom period is where the cultivar gets its name, providing fragrance well into peak Georgia summer.

faqs.question: Do deer eat August Beauty Gardenia?

name: Camellia japonica
water: Moderate — consistent moisture, well-drained soil
description: Camellia japonica is a classic Southern evergreen shrub grown for its large, rose-like flowers, ranging from single to fully double forms in white, pink, red, and bicolor, that bloom during winter and early spring when almost nothing else in the Georgia landscape is flowering. It grows slowly to moderately, eventually reaching 8-12 feet tall and 6-8 feet wide, and thrives in the dappled shade beneath tall pines that are common across Gwinnett County lots, since direct afternoon sun and winter wind can scorch its glossy evergreen foliage. Camellia japonica requires acidic, well-drained soil similar to azaleas and gardenias, and mature plants are notably long-lived, with well-sited specimens surviving many decades in older Southern gardens. Because it blooms in the coldest months, occasional late freezes can brown open flowers, but bud set typically continues over a long winter bloom season so subsequent flushes still open. Its combination of glossy year-round foliage and off-season winter color makes it one of the most valuable shrubs for extending bloom interest beyond the spring and summer season.
plantingTips: Plant Camellia japonica in part shade, ideally with protection from harsh winter wind and afternoon summer sun, in acidic, well-drained soil amended with pine bark fines. Mulch well and avoid deep cultivation near the shallow root zone. Water consistently, especially during dry fall weather when buds are forming for winter bloom. Avoid fertilizing late in the season, which can push tender growth vulnerable to cold damage.

faqs.question: When does Camellia japonica bloom?
faqs.answer: Camellia japonica blooms in winter through early spring, typically December through March in Georgia, providing color when few other shrubs are flowering. This off-season bloom time is one of its biggest landscape values, though occasional hard freezes can brown open flowers on a given flush.

faqs.question: Do deer eat Camellia japonica?
faqs.answer: Yes, Camellia japonica is not considered deer resistant and can be browsed by deer, especially newly planted specimens. In Gwinnett County areas with heavy deer pressure, fencing or repellent application is worth considering until the plant is well established.

name: Camellia sasanqua
water: Moderate — consistent moisture, well-drained soil
description: Camellia sasanqua blooms earlier than Camellia japonica, opening its single-to-semidouble flowers in fall through early winter rather than deep winter into spring, which means the two species together can provide nearly six months of continuous camellia bloom in a single Georgia landscape. It tolerates more sun than Camellia japonica, handling full sun to part shade, and generally grows a bit faster with a looser, more spreading habit that some cultivars can be trained as an espalier or informal hedge. It reaches 6-10 feet tall and 5-7 feet wide and, like all camellias, needs acidic, well-drained soil to perform well in Georgia's clay. Its fall bloom season means flowers coincide with the first cool weather rather than risking the hard freezes that can damage Camellia japonica's late-winter flowers, giving sasanqua slightly more reliable bloom display in most years. Fallen petals carpet the ground attractively beneath the shrub, an ornamental trait Southern gardeners specifically value in shaded fall garden beds.
plantingTips: Plant Camellia sasanqua in full sun to part shade in acidic, well-drained soil amended with pine bark fines; it tolerates more sun than Camellia japonica but still appreciates some afternoon shade in peak Georgia summer heat. Mulch to retain consistent moisture. Water regularly through late summer and early fall as flower buds are forming. Prune, if needed, immediately after flowering finishes in early winter.

faqs.question: What is the difference between Camellia sasanqua and Camellia japonica?
faqs.answer: Camellia sasanqua blooms in fall through early winter and tolerates more sun, while Camellia japonica blooms in winter through early spring and prefers more shade. Growing both provides nearly six months of overlapping camellia bloom color in a single Georgia landscape.

faqs.question: Do deer eat Camellia sasanqua?
