name: Purple Diamond Loropetalum
water: Moderate until established, then drought tolerant
description: Purple Diamond Loropetalum (Loropetalum chinense 'Purple Diamond') is a compact, more manageable-sized loropetalum cultivar that holds its deep burgundy-purple foliage color better year-round than older, larger loropetalum varieties, staying a more predictable 4-6 feet tall and wide rather than the 10-15 feet mature size of unnamed seedling-grown loropetalums often sold decades ago. Fringy hot-pink flowers appear in a heavy spring flush with sporadic rebloom through the growing season, standing out sharply against the dark purple leaves. It tolerates Georgia's clay soil and summer humidity well and, once established, becomes reasonably drought tolerant, needing far less supplemental water than azaleas or hydrangeas planted nearby. Its compact, predictable size makes it much easier to use in foundation plantings and mixed borders than older loropetalum cultivars that quickly outgrew their spot and required constant hard pruning. Purple Diamond is also deer resistant, an advantage over many other flowering shrubs in Gwinnett County landscapes bordering wooded areas with deer pressure.
plantingTips: Plant Purple Diamond Loropetalum in full sun for the best purple foliage color and heaviest bloom, though it tolerates part shade with slightly greener leaves. Amend Georgia clay lightly with compost and mulch well. Water regularly the first growing season; established plants are moderately drought tolerant. Prune lightly after the spring bloom flush if shaping is desired; avoid shearing into a tight ball, which reduces its naturally graceful arching form.

faqs.question: How big does Purple Diamond Loropetalum get?
faqs.answer: Purple Diamond Loropetalum matures to a compact 4-6 feet tall and wide, much smaller and more predictable than older, unnamed loropetalum varieties that can reach 10-15 feet. This makes it far better suited to foundation plantings and smaller garden beds.

faqs.question: Does Purple Diamond Loropetalum need full sun?
faqs.answer: Purple Diamond Loropetalum holds its deepest burgundy-purple foliage color and blooms most heavily in full sun. In part shade it still grows well but the leaves trend more green-purple and flowering is somewhat reduced, so full sun is recommended when foliage color is the priority.

description: Ruby Loropetalum (Loropetalum chinense var. rubrum 'Ruby') is a mid-sized loropetalum cultivar with rich burgundy-red new growth that matures to a deep bronzy-green, offering more color variation across the plant than the more uniformly purple Purple Diamond selection. It grows at a moderate to fast pace to 5-6 feet tall and wide, filling in faster than the more compact Purple Diamond while staying smaller than old, unnamed loropetalum seedlings that can reach 10+ feet. Bright fuchsia-pink, fringe-petaled flowers cover the plant in a heavy spring bloom with lighter rebloom through summer and fall. Ruby Loropetalum handles Georgia's clay soil and summer humidity without issue and, once established, tolerates drought reasonably well. It's deer resistant, an important trait for the many Lawrenceville properties bordering wooded lots. Because its new growth flushes bright red-purple through the growing season, it provides ongoing color contrast against green-leaved companions even outside its main spring bloom window.
plantingTips: Plant Ruby Loropetalum in full sun for the richest foliage color and best bloom; it tolerates part shade with slightly muted color. Georgia clay needs only light amendment. Water regularly through the first season, then reduce as the plant establishes drought tolerance. Prune after the main spring bloom to control size and encourage a fresh flush of colorful new growth.

faqs.question: How is Ruby Loropetalum different from Purple Diamond?
faqs.answer: Ruby Loropetalum grows slightly larger and faster (5-6 ft) than the more compact Purple Diamond (4-6 ft), and its foliage shows more color variation, with bright burgundy-red new growth maturing to bronzy-green rather than staying uniformly deep purple. faqs.question: Is Ruby Loropetalum deer resistant?

name: Crimson Fire Loropetalum

It holds intense reddish-purple foliage color year-round with bright fuchsia-pink spring flowers and light rebloom. Its dwarf habit means it requires far less pruning to maintain a tidy low profile than taller loropetalum types, which need regular size control to stay compact. It tolerates Georgia's clay soil and, once established, handles drought reasonably well, needing only occasional deep watering during extended dry spells. Deer resistance and low maintenance needs make it a practical low-shrub choice for Lawrenceville landscapes wanting consistent purple-red foliage color along a walkway or foundation bed without the size management larger loropetalum cultivars demand.

faqs.answer: Crimson Fire Loropetalum is among the most compact loropetalum cultivars available, staying just 2-3 feet tall and 3-4 feet wide at maturity. name: Knock Out Rose
water: Moderate — drought tolerant once established
description: Knock Out Rose revolutionized landscape rose use when it was introduced because it blooms continuously from spring until frost without the deadheading traditional hybrid tea roses require, and it shows strong resistance to blackspot, the fungal disease that defoliates most roses in Georgia's humid summers. It grows into a rounded, self-cleaning shrub 3-4 feet tall and wide, producing single, cherry-red 3-inch flowers in flushes every 5-6 weeks through the growing season. Full sun, at least 6 hours daily, is essential for the heaviest continuous bloom and the best disease resistance; Knock Out Rose planted in shade blooms less and becomes more susceptible to blackspot and powdery mildew. It tolerates Georgia's clay soil reasonably well provided drainage is adequate, since roses generally dislike standing water at the root zone. Its combination of nearly maintenance-free continuous bloom and strong disease resistance is why Knock Out Rose became one of the best-selling roses in American nursery history and remains a staple of Lawrenceville foundation and border plantings.
plantingTips: Plant Knock Out Rose in full sun, at least 6 hours daily, in well-drained soil; raise the planting site slightly in heavy Georgia clay to prevent root rot. Space plants 3-4 feet apart for a hedge or mass planting. Water deeply weekly the first season; established plants are fairly drought tolerant. Prune back by about a third in late winter to encourage vigorous new growth and the heaviest bloom flush.

faqs.question: Do Knock Out Roses need deadheading?
faqs.answer: No, Knock Out Roses are self-cleaning and drop their spent blooms naturally, so deadheading is not required for continuous flowering. This is a major reason they became so popular, offering repeat bloom from spring through frost with far less maintenance than traditional hybrid tea roses.

faqs.question: How much sun do Knock Out Roses need?
faqs.answer: Knock Out Roses need at least 6 hours of direct sun daily for the heaviest continuous bloom and strongest resistance to blackspot fungal disease. In part shade they still survive but flower less and become more susceptible to disease in Georgia's humid summers.

It grows to the same compact 3-4 feet tall and wide, fitting easily into foundation beds, mixed borders, or mass plantings along a Lawrenceville driveway or walkway. Like the original, it demands full sun, at least 6 hours daily, for its heaviest bloom and best disease resistance, and tolerates Georgia's clay soil well as long as drainage is adequate. Its extended bloom season, flushing roughly every 5-6 weeks from spring until the first hard frost, provides more months of color than almost any other flowering shrub sold in our region, with none of the fungicide spraying traditional roses typically require in humid Southern summers.

name: Butterfly Bush
water: Low to Moderate — drought tolerant once established
description: Butterfly Bush (Buddleja davidii) earns its common name honestly, producing long, fragrant flower spikes from summer through fall that reliably draw swallowtails, monarchs, and other pollinators to a Gwinnett County garden more consistently than almost any other flowering shrub. It grows fast, 2-3 feet per year, reaching 5-8 feet tall and 4-6 feet wide in a single season in good conditions, and blooms on new wood, so it can be cut back hard in late winter without sacrificing summer flowers. It requires full sun and tolerates poor, dry soil well once established, making it a good choice for a hot, sunny spot where fussier shrubs struggle. Note that Buddleja davidii has shown invasive tendencies via self-seeding in some regions of the Southeast; deadheading spent flower spikes before they set seed reduces this risk and also encourages more continuous blooming. Its vigorous growth, deer resistance, and pollinator value make it a popular choice for cutting gardens and butterfly-focused plantings.
plantingTips: Plant Butterfly Bush in full sun in well-drained soil; it tolerates poor, dry Georgia soil once established and does not need rich amendment. Cut back hard, to 12-18 inches, in late winter to encourage vigorous new growth and the best summer bloom, since flowers form on new wood. Deadhead spent flower spikes regularly through summer to encourage continued blooming and reduce self-seeding.

faqs.question: Does Butterfly Bush attract hummingbirds too?
faqs.answer: Yes, Butterfly Bush attracts hummingbirds in addition to butterflies, drawn by its long, nectar-rich flower spikes that bloom continuously from summer through fall. Its combination of pollinator and hummingbird appeal makes it a strong choice for wildlife-focused Georgia gardens.

faqs.question: Should I cut back Butterfly Bush in fall or spring?
faqs.answer: Cut Butterfly Bush back hard in late winter, not fall, to about 12-18 inches from the ground, since it blooms on new wood produced that same season. Pruning in fall removes winter structure without any bloom benefit and can expose cut stems to cold damage.

name: Rose of Sharon
water: Moderate — drought tolerant once established
description: Rose of Sharon (Hibiscus syriacus) is an old-fashioned Southern flowering shrub grown for large, hibiscus-shaped blooms, in white, pink, lavender, or blue-purple depending on variety, that appear continuously through the heat of summer into early fall, a season when many spring-blooming shrubs have long finished flowering. It grows moderately to fast, reaching 8-12 feet tall and 6-10 feet wide, tall enough to use as a small flowering tree or informal screen as well as a border shrub. Rose of Sharon tolerates Georgia's clay soil, heat, and humidity with few problems and, once established, handles drought reasonably well. It self-seeds readily, sometimes producing volunteer seedlings around the base of established plants, so removing spent blooms before they set seed helps control unwanted spread if that is a concern. Its long, reliable summer bloom season when little else is flowering, combined with minimal disease or pest issues in our region, has kept it a staple of older Lawrenceville and Gwinnett County landscapes for generations.
plantingTips: Plant Rose of Sharon in full sun to part shade in well-drained soil; it tolerates Georgia clay without amendment. Space plants 6-8 feet apart if used as an informal screen. Water regularly the first season; established plants tolerate moderate drought. Deadhead spent flowers to reduce self-seeding, and prune in late winter to shape, since it blooms on new wood. Once established in a Gwinnett County landscape, it needs only occasional deep watering during dry stretches rather than a regular irrigation schedule.

faqs.question: Does Rose of Sharon spread or self-seed?
faqs.answer: Yes, Rose of Sharon self-seeds readily and volunteer seedlings often appear around established plants, particularly in mulched beds. Deadheading spent flowers before seed pods form significantly reduces unwanted spread while also encouraging additional blooming through the summer.

faqs.question: Do deer eat Rose of Sharon?
faqs.answer: Yes, Rose of Sharon is not considered deer resistant and can be browsed by deer, especially newly planted specimens. In Gwinnett County areas with heavy deer pressure, fencing or repellent application is worth considering until the plant is well established.

name: Abelia
water: Low to Moderate — drought tolerant once established
description: Abelia (Abelia x grandiflora) is a tough, adaptable flowering shrub with small, glossy leaves and a long season of small, tubular white-to-pink flowers that appear from late spring all the way through fall, providing one of the longest bloom windows of any shrub in a Georgia landscape. It grows into a graceful, arching mound 3-6 feet tall and wide depending on cultivar, some newer selections offer variegated or golden foliage as an added feature beyond the flowers. Abelia is notably drought tolerant once established and tolerates Georgia's clay soil, heat, and humidity with very few pest or disease issues, making it one of the lowest-maintenance flowering shrubs available. Its small flowers are also attractive to bees and butterflies over an extended period. Deer resistance and minimal water needs make it a practical choice for Lawrenceville landscapes wanting reliable, nearly effortless summer-long color without the disease concerns of roses or the fussy soil requirements of azaleas and gardenias.
plantingTips: Plant Abelia in full sun to part shade in well-drained soil; it adapts readily to Georgia clay without heavy amendment. Space plants 3-4 feet apart for a hedge or mass planting. Water regularly the first season; established plants are quite drought tolerant. Prune lightly in late winter to shape, since abelia blooms on new wood and responds well to renewal pruning if it becomes leggy.

faqs.question: How long does Abelia bloom?

This extended bloom time also makes it valuable for pollinators throughout the growing season.

faqs.question: Is Abelia deer resistant?

name: Bloodgood Japanese Maple
sun: Part Shade (morning sun, afternoon shade preferred)
water: Moderate — consistent moisture, avoid drought stress
bloomSeason: N/A (grown for foliage; inconspicuous spring flowers)
description: Bloodgood Japanese Maple (Acer palmatum 'Bloodgood') is the most widely planted red-leaved Japanese maple cultivar in the country, valued for holding deep burgundy-red foliage color through the summer better than many other red maples, which often fade toward green in Georgia's intense heat. It grows slowly to moderately, reaching 15-20 feet tall and wide over many years, with a rounded, layered branching habit that becomes more sculptural with age. Fall color deepens to a brilliant crimson-scarlet before leaf drop. In Zone 8a, afternoon shade is important; Bloodgood tolerates more sun than most Japanese maples but leaf scorch can still occur during peak July and August heat without some afternoon relief, especially in reflected heat near pavement. It prefers consistently moist, well-drained soil and struggles in compacted, poorly drained Georgia clay, so bed preparation matters more for this tree than for tougher natives. As a specimen tree for entryways, courtyards, or as an anchor in a mixed border, Bloodgood remains the benchmark against which other red Japanese maples are compared.
plantingTips: Plant Bloodgood Japanese Maple where it gets morning sun and afternoon shade, especially important during Georgia's hot summers to prevent leaf scorch. Amend heavy clay with compost to improve drainage, since Japanese maples resent wet feet, and mulch well to keep roots cool and moist. Avoid deep planting; the root flare should sit at or slightly above grade. Water consistently during the first two to three years while the root system establishes.

faqs.answer: Bloodgood Japanese Maple tolerates more sun than most Japanese maple cultivars, but in Georgia's Zone 8a heat, afternoon shade helps prevent leaf scorch during July and August. faqs.question: How fast does Bloodgood Japanese Maple grow?
faqs.answer: Bloodgood Japanese Maple grows slowly to moderately, averaging about 1 foot per year, and takes many years to reach its mature size of 15-20 feet tall and wide. Its slow, layered growth habit is part of what makes it valued as a long-term specimen tree.

name: Tamukeyama Japanese Maple
sun: Part Shade (morning sun, afternoon shade preferred)

description: Tamukeyama Japanese Maple (Acer palmatum var. dissectum 'Tamukeyama') is one of the oldest and most cold-hardy weeping laceleaf Japanese maple cultivars still in cultivation, prized for its finely dissected, deep red-purple foliage on a cascading, mushroom-shaped form that stays low and wide, typically 8-10 feet tall but spreading 10-12 feet, rather than growing upright like Bloodgood. Its lacy texture and weeping habit make it a strong focal point near a water feature, entry garden, or Japanese-style planting bed. Tamukeyama holds its reddish-purple color better through summer heat than many other laceleaf cultivars, an important trait in Georgia's intense sun, though afternoon shade is still recommended to prevent leaf scorch. It grows slowly, often less than a foot per year, and is best sited in a protected location out of strong wind, which can damage its delicate dissected leaves. As with all Japanese maples, well-drained soil is essential; this cultivar is particularly unforgiving of soggy, compacted Georgia clay.
plantingTips: Site Tamukeyama Japanese Maple in morning sun with afternoon shade and shelter from strong wind, which can tatter its finely dissected leaves. Plant in well-drained soil raised slightly above grade if your Gwinnett County site has heavy clay, and never let the crown sit in standing water. Mulch to retain moisture and keep roots cool; water consistently through the first several growing seasons.

name: Emperor I Japanese Maple

description: Emperor I Japanese Maple (Acer palmatum 'Wolff', sold as Emperor I) was specifically bred to leaf out later in spring than Bloodgood, avoiding the late frost damage that can burn tender new maple growth during Georgia's unpredictable early spring cold snaps, while also holding its red-purple foliage color reliably through summer heat. It grows at a slightly faster pace than Bloodgood, reaching 15-18 feet tall and 12-15 feet wide with an upright, rounded form. Its later leaf-out is a genuine practical advantage in Zone 8a, where a warm February followed by a hard March freeze regularly damages early-leafing maples. Fall color turns a rich crimson. Like other Japanese maples, Emperor I needs well-drained soil and benefits from afternoon shade protection during peak summer heat, though it tolerates slightly more sun than most cultivars once established. It is a strong alternative to Bloodgood for customers in colder microclimates or frost pockets within Gwinnett County who have lost tender maple growth to late spring freezes in the past.
plantingTips: Plant Emperor I Japanese Maple in morning sun with afternoon shade, in well-drained soil amended if needed for Georgia clay. Its later spring leaf-out reduces frost damage risk, but still avoid low frost-pocket areas of the yard if possible. Mulch to retain moisture and keep roots cool, and water deeply and consistently for the first two to three growing seasons.

description: Coral Bark Japanese Maple (Acer palmatum 'Sango-kaku') offers something few other trees provide: brilliant coral-red bark on young stems that becomes the season's main feature once leaves drop in winter, turning an otherwise bare tree into a striking focal point against a Georgia winter landscape. Its foliage is bright green through spring and summer, taking on gold and orange fall tones before dropping to reveal the vivid stem color, which is most intense on young, vigorous growth and fades somewhat on older wood. It grows at a moderate pace to 15-20 feet tall and 10-15 feet wide, with an upright, somewhat vase-shaped habit. Like other Japanese maples, it needs afternoon shade protection from Georgia's intense summer sun and well-drained soil; leaf scorch on the margins is the most common issue in overly hot, dry, or sunny sites. Periodic renewal pruning of older stems encourages new coral-colored growth, since the brightest bark color occurs on one- to two-year-old wood rather than aged branches.
plantingTips: Plant Coral Bark Japanese Maple in morning sun with afternoon shade, in well-drained soil enriched with compost if planting in heavy Georgia clay. Mulch to retain consistent moisture and prevent heat stress on roots. To maximize winter bark color, prune out a portion of older, duller stems every few years to encourage fresh coral-red new growth, which shows the brightest color.

name: October Glory Red Maple
water: Moderate — drought tolerant once established
description: October Glory Red Maple (Acer rubrum 'October Glory') is a Red Maple cultivar selected for one of the latest and most reliably brilliant fall color displays among shade trees, holding its leaves late into October in Georgia while turning a consistent, vivid scarlet-red, later and more dependable than many seedling-grown red maples that color unevenly or drop early. As a Red Maple, it is native to the Eastern United States including Georgia's Piedmont region, so it is naturally well adapted to our clay soils and tolerates both moist and moderately dry sites, though it prefers more consistent moisture than a true drought-tolerant native. It grows fast, 2-3 feet per year, reaching a substantial 40-50 feet tall and 30-40 feet wide, making it a genuine shade tree suited to larger yards rather than tight urban lots. Its dense, oval canopy provides significant summer shade for a home's south or west side, reducing cooling costs, and its strong branch structure holds up well to Georgia's summer thunderstorms compared to weaker-wooded fast-growing trees.
plantingTips: Plant October Glory Red Maple in full sun to part shade with enough room for its eventual 40-50 foot height and 30-40 foot spread; keep it well away from foundations, driveways, and underground utility lines. It tolerates Georgia clay reasonably well but appreciates consistent moisture, especially the first few years. Stake young trees only if needed for the first year and remove stakes promptly to encourage strong trunk taper.

name: Autumn Blaze Maple

description: Autumn Blaze Maple (Acer x freemanii 'Jeffersred') is a hybrid between Red Maple and Silver Maple that combines the fast growth of Silver Maple, 3-5 feet per year, with the strong wood, brilliant fall color, and disease resistance of Red Maple, avoiding the weak, storm-prone branching that makes true Silver Maple a poor landscape choice. It reaches 50-60 feet tall and 35-40 feet wide, growing into a substantial oval shade tree faster than nearly any other tree of similar mature size. Fall color turns a consistent orange-red, appearing reliably earlier in the season than many other maples. Autumn Blaze is adaptable to a wide range of soil conditions, including Georgia's clay, and tolerates both wetter and drier sites better than most maples once established. Because of its fast growth and eventual large size, it is best suited to bigger Gwinnett County lots where a quick-establishing, long-term shade tree is the goal, planted well clear of the house and any underground utilities.
plantingTips: Plant Autumn Blaze Maple in full sun with ample room for its 50-60 foot mature height and 35-40 foot spread; site it at least 20-25 feet from the house foundation and clear of overhead power lines. It adapts to a range of Georgia soils, including clay, without heavy amendment. Water deeply and regularly the first two to three years to support its very fast growth rate.

name: Brandywine Red Maple
water: Moderate — drought tolerant once established
description: Brandywine Red Maple (Acer rubrum 'Brandywine') is a Red Maple cultivar selected specifically for producing seedless (or nearly seedless) flowers, which means far less of the winged seed litter that other red maples drop on driveways, patios, and lawns each spring, a practical advantage for homeowners tired of cleanup. It also offers outstanding, long-lasting deep red fall color that develops reliably even in years when other maples color unevenly. As a native Red Maple selection, it is well adapted to Georgia's Piedmont clay soils and tolerates a range of moisture conditions from moderately wet to moderately dry. It grows at a moderate to fast pace, reaching 35-45 feet tall and 25-30 feet wide, somewhat more compact than October Glory or Autumn Blaze, making it a good fit for mid-sized Lawrenceville lots that still want a genuine native shade tree without the largest possible mature footprint. Its dense, rounded canopy provides good shade while its lower seed production reduces the volunteer maple seedlings that pop up in garden beds each spring.
plantingTips: Plant Brandywine Red Maple in full sun to part shade with room for its 35-45 foot mature size; it adapts well to Georgia's clay soil and tolerates a range of moisture levels. Water regularly the first two years to establish a strong root system. Its low seed production means less spring cleanup and fewer volunteer seedlings in nearby beds compared to standard red maples.

name: Natchez Crape Myrtle
water: Low to Moderate — drought tolerant once established
description: Natchez Crape Myrtle is widely considered the finest white-flowering crape myrtle cultivar, a National Arboretum introduction bred for mildew resistance and outstanding cinnamon-brown exfoliating bark that provides four-season interest even when the tree is bare in winter. It grows fast, 2-3 feet per year, reaching 20-30 feet tall and 15-20 feet wide, large enough to function as a genuine specimen shade tree rather than just a large shrub. Huge white flower panicles bloom from early summer through early fall, one of the longest bloom seasons of any flowering tree suited to Georgia's climate. Full sun, at least 6 hours daily, is essential for heavy flowering and the best resistance to powdery mildew, a common crape myrtle problem in shadier or crowded plantings. Natchez tolerates Georgia's heat, humidity, and clay soil extremely well once established and needs minimal supplemental water. Because of its large mature size, it is best suited as a specimen or street tree rather than a foundation planting, where topping ('crape murder') is unfortunately common but unnecessary and damaging to the tree's natural vase-shaped form.
plantingTips: Plant Natchez Crape Myrtle in full sun with room for its 20-30 foot mature height and 15-20 foot spread; avoid crowding, which reduces air circulation and increases mildew risk. Georgia clay needs little amendment. Water regularly the first season, then reduce, as established plants are quite drought tolerant. Avoid hard topping ('crape murder'); instead remove only crossing or crowded interior branches in late winter to preserve its natural vase shape.

faqs.question: Why shouldn't you top a crape myrtle?
faqs.answer: Topping, or 'crape murder,' removes the tree's natural vase-shaped structure, encourages weak, whippy regrowth prone to breaking in storms, and reduces flower quality over time. Instead, prune Natchez Crape Myrtle in late winter by removing only crossing, crowded, or damaged branches to preserve its natural form and exfoliating bark display.

faqs.question: How tall does Natchez Crape Myrtle grow?

Its vivid coral-pink color makes it a popular choice for homeowners wanting a bolder color statement than the classic whites and lighter pinks, often planted as a specimen tree or in a row along a driveway for a strong seasonal color display.

name: Southern Magnolia
water: Moderate until established, then drought tolerant
description: Southern Magnolia (Magnolia grandiflora) is the iconic large evergreen tree of the Deep South, native to Georgia and much of the Southeastern Coastal Plain and lower Piedmont, growing eventually to 60-80 feet tall and 30-50 feet wide with massive, glossy dark-green leaves and enormous, intensely fragrant creamy-white flowers up to a foot across from late spring through summer. It is a true specimen tree requiring significant room to reach its full grandeur, and its dense, low-branching habit means it also functions as a substantial privacy and wind screen once mature, though the smaller Little Gem or Bracken's Brown Beauty cultivars fit residential lots far better. As a Georgia native, it is naturally adapted to our clay soils and climate and, once established, becomes quite drought tolerant. Its large leaves drop continuously in a light, year-round litter (not a single fall event), which some homeowners find messy near patios or pools, so siting away from those areas is worth considering. It remains one of the most beloved and recognizable trees in the Southern landscape.
plantingTips: Plant Southern Magnolia with significant clearance, at least 20-30 feet from structures, given its eventual 60-80 foot height and wide, low-branching canopy. It tolerates Georgia clay well once established; water deeply and regularly for the first two to three years. Mulch widely rather than deeply near the trunk, since surface roots are common. Avoid siting directly next to patios or pools due to continuous leaf drop.

Mature size: 60-80 ft tall, 30-50 ft wide — needs a large property

Continuous light leaf drop year-round, not just fall

faqs.question: How big does a Southern Magnolia get?
faqs.answer: Southern Magnolia grows into a massive tree, typically 60-80 feet tall and 30-50 feet wide at full maturity, though it takes many decades to reach that size. Because of this eventual scale, it needs to be planted well away from the house, driveways, and other structures.

faqs.question: Does Southern Magnolia drop leaves in fall?
faqs.answer: Southern Magnolia is evergreen and drops its large, leathery leaves gradually and continuously throughout the year rather than in one concentrated fall event. This ongoing light litter is worth considering when siting the tree away from pools, patios, or manicured lawn areas.

name: White Flowering Dogwood
sun: Part Shade (understory tree, morning sun ideal)
water: Moderate — consistent moisture, avoid drought stress
description: White Flowering Dogwood (Cornus florida) is Georgia's state tree and one of the most beloved native flowering trees in the Southeast, producing a stunning display of large white bracts in early spring before the leaves fully emerge, followed by red berries in fall that are an important food source for birds. As a natural understory tree found throughout Georgia's Piedmont forests, it performs best in the dappled morning sun and afternoon shade found at a woodland edge rather than full, exposed sun, which stresses it and increases susceptibility to powdery mildew and dogwood borer. It grows slowly to moderately, reaching 20-30 feet tall and 20-25 feet wide with a graceful, horizontally-tiered branching habit. Georgia's dogwoods have faced pressure in recent decades from dogwood anthracnose, a fungal disease more prevalent at higher elevations and in wetter, shadier sites; Piedmont plantings with good air circulation and morning sun generally see fewer problems. Fall color adds burgundy-red foliage to its seasonal interest beyond the iconic spring bloom.
plantingTips: Plant White Flowering Dogwood where it gets morning sun and afternoon shade, mimicking its natural woodland-edge habitat; avoid full, exposed all-day sun, which increases stress and disease susceptibility. Amend Georgia clay with compost for better drainage, and mulch widely to protect its shallow root system without piling mulch against the trunk. Water consistently, especially during dry spells, since drought stress is the leading cause of borer and disease problems.
fastFacts: Georgia's state tree, native understory species
Mature size: 20-30 ft tall, 20-25 ft wide
Large white spring bracts before leaves emerge
Red fall berries are an important bird food source
Prefers morning sun, afternoon shade (woodland-edge conditions)
Not deer resistant; susceptible to stress-related borers and disease

faqs.question: Why is my dogwood tree struggling in full sun?
faqs.answer: Flowering Dogwood is naturally an understory tree adapted to dappled woodland light, and full, exposed sun combined with drought stress makes it significantly more vulnerable to powdery mildew and dogwood borer. Morning sun with afternoon shade, consistent moisture, and good mulching closely mimic its natural growing conditions and reduce these problems.

faqs.question: Is White Flowering Dogwood native to Georgia?
faqs.answer: Yes, White Flowering Dogwood (Cornus florida) is native throughout Georgia and is officially the state tree, commonly found as an understory tree in Piedmont forests. Its native status makes it well suited to Georgia's clay soils when planted in appropriate dappled shade conditions.

name: Pink Flowering Dogwood
sun: Part Shade (understory tree, morning sun ideal)
water: Moderate — consistent moisture, avoid drought stress
description: Pink Flowering Dogwood (Cornus florida f. rubra) is a pink-bracted form of Georgia's native flowering dogwood, offering the same iconic early spring bloom, tiered horizontal branching, and fall red berries as the white species type, but with bracts ranging from soft blush pink to a deeper rose depending on the specific cultivar. It shares the same understory growing preferences as white dogwood, performing best with morning sun and afternoon shade rather than full, exposed sun, and the same susceptibility to stress-related powdery mildew and dogwood borer if planted in poor conditions. It grows slowly to moderately, reaching 20-25 feet tall and wide, and provides valuable early-season color that pairs beautifully against the white blooms of Eastern Redbud's cousin or the deeper magenta of Redbud itself, both of which bloom around the same time in the Georgia Piedmont. Its fall foliage also turns an attractive burgundy-red. Pink Flowering Dogwood is a favorite for adding color variety to native spring plantings beyond the classic white dogwood.
plantingTips: Plant Pink Flowering Dogwood in morning sun with afternoon shade, mimicking its natural woodland-edge habitat, and amend Georgia clay with compost for improved drainage. Mulch widely without piling against the trunk to protect its shallow roots. Water consistently, especially during dry periods, since drought-stressed dogwoods are far more prone to borer damage and disease in our climate. Once established in a Gwinnett County landscape, it needs only occasional deep watering during dry stretches rather than a regular irrigation schedule.

Blooms early spring before leaves emerge

faqs.question: Is Pink Flowering Dogwood the same species as white dogwood?
faqs.answer: Yes, Pink Flowering Dogwood is a pink-bracted form (Cornus florida f. rubra) of the same native species as White Flowering Dogwood, sharing identical growth habits, bloom timing, and understory light preferences. The main difference is bract color, ranging from blush pink to deeper rose depending on the cultivar.

faqs.question: Is Pink Flowering Dogwood native to Georgia?
faqs.answer: Yes, Pink Flowering Dogwood is native to Georgia and the Southeastern United States, which makes it naturally well adapted to the region's clay soils, summer humidity, and Zone 8a climate. Native status generally means less supplemental water and fertilizer are needed once the plant is established in a Lawrenceville landscape.

name: Kousa Dogwood
water: Moderate — consistent moisture, avoid drought stress
bloomSeason: Late Spring (2-3 weeks after native dogwood)
description: Kousa Dogwood (Cornus kousa) is an Asian dogwood species that blooms two to three weeks later than native White Flowering Dogwood, extending the dogwood bloom season into late spring, and offers significantly better resistance to dogwood anthracnose and borer problems that affect the native species in stressed conditions. Its pointed white (or pink in some cultivars) bracts sit upright above the foliage rather than facing outward like native dogwood, giving a distinctly different, layered look, and it produces unusual raspberry-like red fruit in late summer that is edible, though rarely eaten by humans, and attractive to wildlife. It tolerates more full sun than native dogwood, an important practical advantage for open Lawrenceville lots without mature tree canopy to provide the dappled shade native dogwood prefers. Bark exfoliates attractively with age, adding winter interest. Growing slowly to moderately to 20-30 feet tall and wide, Kousa Dogwood has become an increasingly popular alternative to native dogwood specifically because of its improved disease resistance and sun tolerance.
plantingTips: Plant Kousa Dogwood in full sun to part shade; unlike native White Flowering Dogwood, it tolerates considerably more direct sun, making it a better fit for open, sunnier Lawrenceville lots. Amend Georgia clay with compost for drainage and mulch widely to protect its root zone. Water consistently through establishment; while more disease resistant than native dogwood, it still benefits from reduced drought stress.

faqs.question: Is Kousa Dogwood better than native dogwood?
faqs.answer: Kousa Dogwood offers significantly better resistance to anthracnose and borer problems than native White Flowering Dogwood, plus tolerance for more direct sun, making it a more forgiving choice for open, sunny yards. Native dogwood, however, better supports local wildlife and has deeper ecological ties to Georgia's native ecosystem.

faqs.question: Can you eat Kousa Dogwood fruit?
faqs.answer: Yes, Kousa Dogwood produces raspberry-like red fruit in late summer that is technically edible, with a sweet, custard-like flavor, though it's rarely eaten by people due to its large seeds and grainy texture. Birds and wildlife readily consume the fruit instead.

name: Yoshino Cherry
water: Moderate — consistent moisture, avoid drought stress
description: Yoshino Cherry (Prunus x yedoensis) is the flowering cherry famous for Washington D.C.'s Tidal Basin display, producing a spectacular flush of pale pink to white, lightly fragrant blossoms that cover the entire tree for two to three weeks in early spring before the leaves emerge. It grows relatively fast for a flowering tree, about 2 feet per year, reaching 30-40 feet tall and 25-30 feet wide with a broad, rounded canopy, making it a substantial specimen or shade tree in addition to its spring flower display. Yoshino Cherry performs well in Georgia's Zone 8a climate and tolerates our clay soil provided drainage is adequate, since flowering cherries are prone to root and crown rot in constantly wet conditions. It is relatively short-lived compared to oaks or maples, typically 20-30 years, and can be susceptible to borers and canker, especially if stressed by drought or mechanical damage to the trunk. Despite these maintenance considerations, its dramatic, brief spring display makes it one of the most requested ornamental flowering trees for entryways and focal points in Lawrenceville landscapes.
plantingTips: Plant Yoshino Cherry in full sun to part shade in well-drained soil; raise the planting site in heavy Georgia clay to avoid root and crown rot. Avoid mower and trimmer damage to the trunk base, which invites borers and canker, the tree's most common problems. Water consistently through establishment and during summer dry spells, and avoid heavy pruning except to remove dead or crossing wood in late winter.

faqs.question: How long does Yoshino Cherry bloom?
faqs.answer: Yoshino Cherry blooms for about two to three weeks in early spring, typically March in the Atlanta metro area, producing a dramatic flush of pale pink to white blossoms before the leaves emerge. The exact bloom window shifts slightly year to year depending on early spring temperatures.

faqs.question: How long do Yoshino Cherry trees live?
faqs.answer: Yoshino Cherry trees typically live 20-30 years, shorter than long-lived shade trees like oaks or maples, and are prone to borers and canker especially when stressed by trunk damage or drought. Avoiding mower and trimmer injury near the base significantly extends the tree's healthy lifespan.

name: Eastern Redbud
water: Moderate — drought tolerant once established
description: Eastern Redbud (Cercis canadensis) is a native understory tree found throughout Georgia's forests, instantly recognizable each early spring when clusters of small magenta-pink flowers cover its bare branches before the heart-shaped leaves emerge, often described as the Southern woodland's first true burst of spring color, appearing around the same time as White Flowering Dogwood. It grows at a moderate pace to 20-30 feet tall and 20-25 feet wide with a graceful, often multi-trunked or spreading form, and adapts to both full sun and considerable shade, tolerating Georgia's clay soils and periodic drought better than many ornamental flowering trees since it is a genuine native. Its flowers are also edible and were historically used in Southern cooking, and it is an early-season nectar source for native bees. Fall color turns a soft yellow. Eastern Redbud is a lower-maintenance, longer-lived alternative to Yoshino Cherry for customers wanting native spring flower color with better drought tolerance and fewer pest and disease concerns.
plantingTips: Plant Eastern Redbud in full sun to part shade; it tolerates Georgia clay and periodic drought better than most flowering trees once established. Water regularly the first two seasons to establish a strong root system, then reduce, as mature trees are quite drought tolerant. Redbuds have a naturally graceful, sometimes irregular branching habit that generally needs little corrective pruning beyond removing crossing branches.

faqs.question: Is Eastern Redbud native to Georgia?
faqs.answer: Yes, Eastern Redbud (Cercis canadensis) is native throughout Georgia, commonly found as an understory tree in Piedmont forests alongside White Flowering Dogwood. Its native status makes it well adapted to local clay soils and more drought tolerant than many non-native ornamental flowering trees once established.

faqs.question: When does Eastern Redbud bloom?
faqs.answer: Eastern Redbud blooms in early spring, typically March in the Atlanta metro area, producing clusters of magenta-pink flowers directly on bare branches and even old trunk wood before the heart-shaped leaves emerge. It blooms around the same general time as native dogwood, providing an early splash of woodland color.

name: Forest Pansy Redbud
water: Moderate — drought tolerant once established
description: Forest Pansy Redbud (Cercis canadensis 'Forest Pansy') is a native Eastern Redbud cultivar selected for its striking reddish-purple heart-shaped foliage, which emerges deep burgundy in spring and holds substantial color through summer before shifting to bronze-green, giving it season-long foliage interest well beyond the magenta-pink spring flowers all redbuds share. It grows at a moderate pace to a slightly more compact 20-25 feet tall and 15-20 feet wide compared to the straight species. Because its foliage color is the main draw, siting matters: some afternoon shade in Georgia's intense summer sun helps prevent leaf scorch and keeps the purple color from fading toward green as quickly as it would in full, exposed sun all day. As a native species selection, it retains the same clay soil adaptability and drought tolerance once established as standard Eastern Redbud. Its combination of native heritage, spring flowers, and season-long purple foliage color has made Forest Pansy one of the most popular small ornamental trees for Lawrenceville landscapes wanting more than a single bloom season of interest.
plantingTips: Plant Forest Pansy Redbud in full sun to part shade; afternoon shade helps preserve the deepest purple foliage color through Georgia's hot summers and reduces leaf scorch risk. It tolerates clay soil well and, once established, handles periodic drought better than most ornamental trees. Water regularly the first two seasons while establishing. Once established in a Gwinnett County landscape, it needs only occasional deep watering during dry stretches rather than a regular irrigation schedule.

faqs.question: Does Forest Pansy Redbud need shade for its purple color?
faqs.answer: Forest Pansy Redbud holds its deepest reddish-purple foliage color best with some afternoon shade in Georgia's intense summer sun; all-day full sun can cause the color to fade toward bronze-green faster and increases the risk of leaf scorch. Morning sun with afternoon shade is the ideal balance.

faqs.question: Is Forest Pansy Redbud native to Georgia?
faqs.answer: Yes, Forest Pansy Redbud is native to Georgia and the Southeastern United States, which makes it naturally well adapted to the region's clay soils, summer humidity, and Zone 8a climate. Native status generally means less supplemental water and fertilizer are needed once the plant is established in a Lawrenceville landscape.

name: Encore Autumn Angel Azalea
water: Moderate — regular water, avoid drought stress
description: Encore Autumn Angel Azalea is one of the most compact plants in the Encore repeat-blooming series, staying a tidy 2-3 feet tall and wide while producing clean white, ruffled flowers across spring, summer, and fall blooms rather than the single spring flush of traditional azaleas. Its smaller mature size makes it especially useful for foundation plantings and container culture on patios where larger Encore varieties would eventually crowd the space. Like all Encore Azaleas, it tolerates more direct sun than older Southern azalea varieties, with 4-6 hours of sun actually encouraging heavier reblooming, while still adapting to the part shade found under Georgia's mature tree canopy. It requires the same acidic, well-drained, evenly moist soil all azaleas need, and Gwinnett County's naturally acidic clay is generally well suited once drainage is improved with organic matter. White-flowering azaleas like Autumn Angel are especially valued for brightening shaded garden corners and for pairing with brighter-colored Encore varieties in mixed plantings without clashing.
plantingTips: Plant in a bed amended with pine bark fines for drainage and acidity; set the root ball slightly above grade in Georgia clay and mulch 2-3 inches deep. Provide 4-6 hours of sun for the best repeat bloom. Water deeply twice weekly during summer heat since azalea roots are shallow and drought-sensitive. Avoid deep cultivation near the root zone. Once established in a Gwinnett County landscape, it needs only occasional deep watering during dry stretches rather than a regular irrigation schedule.

faqs.question: How big does Encore Autumn Angel Azalea get?
faqs.answer: Encore Autumn Angel Azalea stays compact at 2-3 feet tall and wide, one of the smallest plants in the Encore series. This makes it well suited to foundation plantings, smaller garden beds, and container growing where larger azalea varieties would eventually outgrow the space.

faqs.question: Do deer eat Encore Autumn Angel Azalea?
faqs.answer: Yes, Encore Autumn Angel Azalea is not considered deer resistant and can be browsed by deer, especially newly planted specimens. In Gwinnett County areas with heavy deer pressure, fencing or repellent application is worth considering until the plant is well established.

name: Encore Autumn Bonfire Azalea
water: Moderate — regular water, avoid drought stress
description: Encore Autumn Bonfire Azalea delivers one of the most vivid true-red flower colors in the repeat-blooming Encore series, covering the plant in bright red-orange blooms across three separate bloom cycles each year rather than azaleas' typical single spring show. It grows into a rounded shrub 3-4 feet tall and wide and, like other Encore varieties, tolerates significantly more sun than traditional Southern azaleas, with more sun exposure actually encouraging heavier summer and fall reblooming rather than causing stress. It needs the same acidic, evenly moist, well-drained soil azaleas require throughout, and Gwinnett County gardeners should amend heavy clay with pine bark fines to ensure adequate drainage, since azalea roots are shallow and quickly damaged by both waterlogging and drought. Its bold red color makes it a strong focal point in mixed shrub borders, especially paired with the white or purple tones of other Encore cultivars for high-contrast seasonal color that lasts far longer than a single spring bloom window.
plantingTips: Amend planting beds with pine bark fines for drainage and acidity, and set the root ball slightly high in Georgia clay. Provide 4-6 hours of sun for the heaviest repeat bloom. Mulch 2-3 inches deep and water deeply twice weekly during summer heat, since shallow azalea roots stress quickly under drought. Once established in a Gwinnett County landscape, it needs only occasional deep watering during dry stretches rather than a regular irrigation schedule.

name: Encore Autumn Royalty Azalea
water: Moderate — regular water, avoid drought stress
description: Encore Autumn Royalty Azalea is among the original and most cold-hardy cultivars in the Encore repeat-blooming series, producing large, vivid purple-magenta flowers across spring, summer, and fall bloom cycles on a larger-growing shrub that reaches 4-5 feet tall and wide, sizable enough to use as a specimen or informal hedge rather than only a foundation planting. It needs acidic, well-drained, consistently moist soil, and its bold purple-magenta color makes a striking contrast when paired with white or soft pink Encore cultivars in a mixed azalea planting bed.

Mulch well and water deeply twice weekly in summer heat, since azalea roots are shallow and sensitive to drought stress. Once established in a Gwinnett County landscape, it needs only occasional deep watering during dry stretches rather than a regular irrigation schedule.

name: George Tabor Azalea
water: Moderate — consistent moisture, avoid drought stress
description: George Tabor Azalea is one of the largest and most vigorous of the classic Southern Indica azalea group, a set of large-growing, single-flush spring bloomers that have anchored Southern gardens for generations, reaching an eventual 6-10 feet tall and 6-8 feet wide, tall enough to use as a flowering privacy hedge or specimen rather than a small foundation shrub. Like all traditional azaleas, it thrives in the dappled shade under Georgia pines and hardwoods and requires acidic, well-drained, consistently moist soil, and its shallow, fibrous roots make it sensitive to both drought and compacted clay. Its larger mature size compared to Encore or dwarf azalea varieties makes George Tabor a good choice for Lawrenceville homeowners wanting a substantial, old-fashioned spring flowering hedge along a wooded property line rather than a smaller, repeat-blooming foundation plant.
plantingTips: Plant George Tabor Azalea in part shade to filtered light, avoiding hot afternoon sun. Amend Georgia clay with pine bark fines for acidity and drainage, set the root ball slightly high, and mulch well. Space plants 5-6 feet apart if used as a flowering hedge, given its large mature size. Water consistently through the first two growing seasons and during summer dry spells thereafter.

name: Formosa Azalea
water: Moderate — consistent moisture, avoid drought stress
description: Formosa Azalea is one of the oldest and most widely planted Southern Indica azaleas, a mainstay of historic Southern gardens for well over a century, known for its enormous magenta-purple flowers, among the largest of any azalea, that can nearly cover the entire shrub during its single, dramatic spring bloom. It grows large and vigorously, reaching 6-10 feet tall and equally wide over time, making it suitable for a substantial flowering hedge, screen, or specimen planting rather than a compact foundation shrub. Like other traditional azaleas, it performs best in the dappled shade beneath Georgia's pines and hardwoods and needs acidic, well-drained, evenly moist soil to thrive; its shallow root system is easily stressed by both drought and heavy, compacted clay. Formosa Azalea's bold magenta-purple color makes an especially striking spring display against a backdrop of dark evergreens, and many older Gwinnett County properties still feature decades-old Formosa plantings that bloom reliably every spring with minimal intervention.
plantingTips: Plant Formosa Azalea in part shade to filtered light in acidic, well-drained soil amended with pine bark fines; avoid hot afternoon sun exposure. Space plants 6-8 feet apart given its large eventual size if used as a hedge or mass planting. Water consistently through establishment, and mulch well to protect the shallow root system from Georgia's summer heat. Once established in a Gwinnett County landscape, it needs only occasional deep watering during dry stretches rather than a regular irrigation schedule.

name: Kleim's Hardy Gardenia
water: Moderate — consistent moisture, well-drained soil
description: Kleim's Hardy Gardenia is a compact, notably cold-hardy gardenia selection with smaller leaves and a lower, more spreading habit than standard Gardenia jasminoides, staying just 2-3 feet tall but spreading 3-4 feet wide, which makes it a useful low-growing fragrant groundcover-style planting rather than a taller specimen shrub. Its improved cold tolerance compared to standard gardenia varieties makes it more reliable through Georgia's occasional hard winter snaps, an important advantage for gardeners who have lost less hardy gardenias to a severe cold event. It produces smaller but still intensely fragrant single white flowers in a concentrated late-spring bloom rather than the extended bloom season of cultivars like August Beauty. Like all gardenias, it requires acidic, well-drained, evenly moist soil, and its lower, wider habit makes it particularly useful for edging a walkway or filling a foreground bed where its fragrance can be enjoyed at close range without a tall shrub blocking the view behind it.
plantingTips: Plant Kleim's Hardy Gardenia in full sun to part shade in acidic, well-drained soil amended with pine bark fines. Mulch to retain even soil moisture. Its lower, spreading habit works well as a low border or foreground planting; space plants 3 feet apart for a continuous low hedge. Fertilize in spring with an acid-forming fertilizer to support the late-spring bloom.

name: Patriot Hosta
water: Moderate to High — consistent moisture
description: Patriot Hosta is a variegated hosta cultivar with bold dark-green leaves edged in a crisp white margin, providing strong visual contrast in the shaded beds beneath Georgia's mature oaks and pines where hostas are among the most reliable perennial foliage plants available. It forms a clump 1.5-2 feet tall and 2-3 feet wide, expanding gradually each year, and sends up lavender flower spikes in summer, though the variegated foliage is the main ornamental draw. Hostas need consistent moisture and appreciate Georgia's humid summers as long as soil doesn't dry out completely between waterings, and they perform best in part to full shade since direct afternoon sun scorches their leaf margins, especially on variegated types like Patriot. The most persistent challenge growing hostas in the Southeast is slug and deer damage; deer will readily browse hosta foliage, so plantings near wooded property lines with deer pressure often need protection. Its bold white-edged foliage makes Patriot Hosta a dependable, long-lived anchor for shaded perennial borders.
plantingTips: Plant Patriot Hosta in part to full shade in soil enriched with compost to retain consistent moisture; Georgia clay benefits from organic matter to improve both drainage and water-holding capacity. Mulch to conserve moisture and suppress weeds. Water regularly during dry spells, since hostas wilt quickly without consistent moisture. Watch for slug damage and consider deer protection in wooded areas.

faqs.question: How much water does Patriot Hosta need?

name: Francee Hosta

Summer brings tall lavender flower spikes above the foliage mound. Deer and slugs are the primary challenges growing hostas in the Southeast; Francee's faster growth rate helps it recover more quickly from browsing damage than slower-growing hosta cultivars.

Mulch to conserve moisture. Divide clumps every 3-4 years in early spring or fall to control size and create new plants. Water during dry spells and monitor for slug damage on the foliage. name: Blue Angel Hosta
water: Moderate to High — consistent moisture
description: Blue Angel Hosta is one of the largest blue-leaved hosta cultivars available, forming a massive mound of thick, powdery blue-green heart-shaped leaves that can reach 2.5-3 feet tall and spread an impressive 4-5 feet wide at maturity, making a dramatic focal-point statement in a large shaded bed rather than a background filler plant. Its thick, substantial leaves are somewhat more slug resistant than thinner-leaved hosta cultivars, an advantage in Georgia's humid climate where slugs are a persistent hosta pest. Tall white flower spikes rise above the foliage in summer. Like all hostas, Blue Angel needs part to full shade and consistent soil moisture to look its best; the powdery blue coating (bloom) on its leaves is also more pronounced in lower light and can wash off with excessive overhead watering or heavy rain, so siting under some tree canopy protection helps preserve the blue coloring longer into the season. Water consistently and watch for slug damage, though its thick leaves resist slugs better than thinner hosta varieties.

Native species of Heuchera occur in parts of the Eastern United States, and garden cultivars generally perform well in Zone 8a with part shade and well-drained soil. Delicate, airy flower spikes rise above the foliage mound in late spring through summer, attracting hummingbirds and small pollinators. Heuchera is notably deer resistant, a valuable trait for Gwinnett County properties bordering wooded areas, and unlike hostas, it is rarely bothered by deer browsing, making it a reliable low-maintenance foliage accent where deer pressure limits other shade perennial choices.

name: Autumn Fern
water: Moderate — consistent moisture, tolerates some drought once established
description: Autumn Fern (Dryopteris erythrosora) gets its common name from the coppery-orange color of its new spring fronds, a striking contrast to the deep glossy green they mature into by summer, giving this evergreen-to-semi-evergreen fern more seasonal color interest than most shade ferns. It forms a tidy clump 1.5-2 feet tall and wide and, unlike many ferns, tolerates Georgia's clay soil reasonably well once established, along with brief dry spells better than more moisture-demanding fern species. It is one of the more sun-tolerant ferns available, handling filtered morning light in addition to the deeper shade most ferns require, and it holds its fronds through much of a mild Georgia winter rather than dying back completely. Autumn Fern is also notably deer resistant, an important advantage in wooded Lawrenceville landscapes, making it one of the few reliably deer-proof foliage plants for shaded beds alongside Heuchera. Its coppery new growth pairs beautifully with the burgundy tones of Encore Azalea or Loropetalum in a mixed shade border.

Divide clumps in early spring if needed to control size.

name: Miss Huff Lantana
water: Low — very drought tolerant once established
growthRate: Fast (returns from roots each spring, dies to ground in winter)
description: Miss Huff Lantana is the most cold-hardy lantana cultivar commonly grown as a perennial in Zone 8a Georgia, reliably dying back to the ground each winter and resprouting from its root system the following spring rather than needing replacement like tender annual lantana varieties. It grows fast once warm weather arrives, reaching 4-6 feet tall and wide in a single season, and produces clusters of orange, coral, and yellow flowers continuously from late spring until the first hard frost, making it one of the longest and most reliable bloom seasons of any perennial in a Georgia landscape. It is highly drought tolerant once established and thrives in poor, hot, sunny sites where fussier perennials struggle, requiring essentially no supplemental water except during extended drought. Its flowers are a strong butterfly and pollinator magnet throughout the growing season. Because it dies back completely each winter, gardeners should cut the dead stems back to the ground in late winter before new spring growth emerges from the crown.
plantingTips: Plant Miss Huff Lantana in full sun in well-drained soil; it tolerates poor, dry Georgia soil and needs no rich amendment. Cut the dead top growth back to the ground in late winter after the last hard freeze, since it resprouts from the roots each spring. Water regularly the first season for establishment; afterward it is highly drought tolerant. Once established in a Gwinnett County landscape, it needs only occasional deep watering during dry stretches rather than a regular irrigation schedule.

faqs.question: Is lantana toxic to dogs?
faqs.answer: Yes, Lantana, including Miss Huff, contains toxic compounds in its leaves and unripe berries that can cause gastrointestinal upset and, in serious cases, liver damage if ingested by dogs or cats. Keep pets from grazing on lantana foliage and berries in the landscape.

It is extremely drought tolerant once established, thriving in hot, sunny, poor-soil locations, and its dense, spreading habit makes it effective as a flowering groundcover along a sunny slope or bed edge, suppressing weeds while blooming continuously. Like all lantana, its nectar-rich flowers strongly attract butterflies and other pollinators throughout the growing season, and its low, wide form contrasts nicely with taller, upright perennials in a mixed sunny border.
plantingTips: Plant New Gold Lantana in full sun in well-drained soil; it thrives in poor, dry conditions and needs no rich amendment. name: Hot Lips Salvia

description: Hot Lips Salvia (Salvia microphylla 'Hot Lips') is famous for its distinctive bicolor flowers, red and white on the same bloom, and sometimes on the same plant simultaneously, that appear almost continuously from late spring until the first hard frost, giving it one of the longest bloom seasons of any perennial salvia grown in Georgia. It grows into a rounded, shrubby mound 2-3 feet tall and wide with small, aromatic leaves, and the flower color pattern can shift with temperature, running more solid red in hot summer weather and more distinctly bicolor in cooler spring and fall conditions. Pet safe, technically edible though bred for appearance
Declines once Georgia spring heat arrives

faqs.question: Does cold weather hurt ornamental kale?
faqs.answer: No, Ornamental Kale actually develops more vivid purple, pink, and cream foliage color in response to cold temperatures and frost, making it one of the few plants that improves in appearance through a Georgia winter rather than declining. It reliably tolerates hard freezes and even light snow with minimal damage.

faqs.question: Do deer eat Ornamental Kale?
faqs.answer: Yes, Ornamental Kale is not considered deer resistant and can be browsed by deer, especially newly planted specimens. In Gwinnett County areas with heavy deer pressure, fencing or repellent application is worth considering until the plant is well established.
